tibur.t: Latin city above the falls of the Aniene, a member of the Latin League that kept its independence as a Roman ally after 338 BCE.
tibur.o: Tibur, modern Tivoli, stood on a ridge where the Aniene river drops from the hills into the plain east of Rome. Legend claimed Greek founders, three Argive brothers including Tiburtus. Settlement goes back to the early Iron Age, and by the 6th century BCE it was one of the stronger Latin towns.
tibur.r: Tibur controlled the routes from Rome into the central Apennines and quarried travertine. Its great sanctuary of Hercules Victor drew traders and pilgrims. As a member of the Latin League it often acted independently of Rome, and in the 360s and 350s BCE it allied with the Gauls against Rome.
tibur.e: Tibur fought on the Latin side in the Latin War of 340–338 BCE and lost territory, but unlike most Latin towns it kept independence as a Roman ally until citizenship came after the Social War. It became a resort for Roman aristocrats and the site of Hadrian's Villa.

twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A Delta dynasty from Mendes that kept Egypt independent of Persia in the early 4th century BCE through Greek alliances.
twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Around 399 to 398 BCE Nepherites I, a general from Mendes in the central Delta, overthrew Amyrtaeus of the Twenty-eighth Dynasty of Egypt and founded a new line. He sent grain and ships to Sparta, then at war with Persia, and built at Karnak and Mendes.
twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The dynasty's strongest king, Hakor (Achoris), ruled for about thirteen years. He allied with Evagoras of Cyprus and Athens, hired Greek mercenaries under the Athenian Chabrias and repelled a Persian attack around 385 to 383 BCE. He was an active builder, restoring temples across Egypt. Rivalry between family branches weakened the throne, with short reigns by Psammuthes and Nepherites II.
twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: In 380 BCE Nectanebo I, a general from Sebennytos, deposed Nepherites II and founded the Thirtieth Dynasty of Egypt. The remains of a royal tomb at Mendes, probably that of Nepherites I, have been excavated, and Hakor's building works were often reinscribed by his successors.

twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The Libyan pharaohs of Bubastis, founded by Sheshonq I, the biblical Shishak, whose realm gradually split into rival kingdoms.
twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Sheshonq I, Great Chief of the Ma and descendant of Meshwesh settlers at Bubastis, succeeded the Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt around 943 BCE. He reunited the country by appointing his sons to key posts, including the high priesthood of Amun at Thebes.
twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Sheshonq I campaigned in Palestine around 925 BCE, recorded on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak and in the Bible as the attack of Shishak on Jerusalem. Osorkon I and Osorkon II endowed temples lavishly, and Osorkon II rebuilt at Bubastis. Royal princes held regional commands, so the state became a network of Libyan family fiefs. Under Takelot II, Thebes rebelled against Prince Osorkon, as his chronicle at Karnak records.
twenty-second-dynasty-of-egypt.e: From about 837 BCE rival kings appeared, including the Twenty-third Dynasty of Egypt, and the realm fragmented. Piye's invasion around 728 BCE reduced the dynasty to a minor Delta kingship, and its last kings disappeared under the Kushite Empire around 720 BCE.

taifa-of-beja-and-evora.t: A short-lived state of the Banu Wazir in the Alentejo, one of the regimes that rose on the ruins of Almoravid power in the 1140s.
taifa-of-beja-and-evora.o: In 1144 Sidray ibn Wazir, a commander of a local family, took Beja and Évora in the revolt against the Almoravids. At first an ally of Ibn Qasi of the Second Taifa of Mértola, he soon broke with him, while his relatives held the Second Taifa of Badajoz.
taifa-of-beja-and-evora.r: The territory covered the wheat lands of the Alentejo between the Tagus and the Algarve, a frontier exposed to raids from the Kingdom of Portugal. Sidray ruled as a military strongman and became one of the leading figures of the western revolt.
taifa-of-beja-and-evora.e: Around 1150 Sidray submitted to the Almohads, who kept him as a governor. Évora was captured for Portugal in 1165 by Gerald the Fearless, and Beja was taken definitively in 1234.

trinovantes.t: Essex people whose alliance with Julius Caesar made them Rome's first British treaty partners, and who later rose with Boudica against Camulodunum.
trinovantes.o: The Trinovantes first appear in Caesar's account of 54 BCE, when their prince Mandubracius, whose father had been killed by Cassivellaunus, fled to Caesar in Gaul. Caesar restored him and forbade Cassivellaunus to harm them, making the Trinovantes the earliest British people bound to Rome by agreement.
trinovantes.r: Their land in Essex and southern Suffolk was rich farmland with close links to the Continent. Rulers such as Addedomarus and Dubnovellaunus issued gold coins, and Camulodunum grew into a vast oppidum defended by long dykes, with burials like the Lexden tumulus holding Roman luxury goods. Around 10 CE the Catuvellaunian king Cunobelinus took Camulodunum and made it his capital.
trinovantes.e: After the Claudian invasion of 43, Camulodunum became the first capital of Roman Britain and from 49 a colony of veterans who seized Trinovantian land. Resentment led the Trinovantes to join Boudica of the Iceni in 60 or 61, when Camulodunum was burned. Afterwards they formed a civitas in the Roman province.

tiwanaku.t: A highland civilisation near Lake Titicaca whose monumental city and religious art dominated the southern Andes for half a millennium before the Incas.
tiwanaku.o: Tiwanaku began as a village south of Lake Titicaca in present-day Bolivia in the last centuries BCE and grew into a major ceremonial city by about 500 CE, filling the space left by Pukará. At 3,850 metres, it is one of the highest cities ever built.
tiwanaku.r: Tiwanaku was ruled by an elite closely tied to religion, centred on monuments such as the Akapana pyramid, the Kalasasaya platform with the Gateway of the Sun, and the Semi-Subterranean Temple. Raised-field farming by the lake, llama caravans and colonies in warmer valleys such as Moquegua supplied the city. Its Staff God imagery spread across the southern Andes. At its height the city may have held 20,000 people or more.
tiwanaku.e: Tiwanaku collapsed around 1000 to 1100, probably after a long drought undermined lake-shore agriculture. The region broke up into Aymara kingdoms such as the Lupaca Kingdom and Colla Kingdom. The Incas later regarded Titicaca as their place of origin. Tiwanaku became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

taifa-of-valencia.t: A rich taifa on the Valencian huerta, governed by Amirid heirs and later by Toledo, whose fall ended with El Cid's conquest of the city in 1094.
taifa-of-valencia.o: In 1010-1011 the freedmen Mubarak and Muzaffar took control of Valencia as the Caliphate of Córdoba disintegrated. In 1021 the city recognised Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Amir, a grandson of the regent al-Mansur, whose family ruled until 1065.
taifa-of-valencia.r: Valencia drew wealth from irrigated huerta farming, rice, silk and its port. Abd al-Aziz (1021-1061) was a capable ruler who also controlled Almería for a time. In 1065 al-Mamun of the Taifa of Toledo annexed the city, and after Toledo fell in 1085 Alfonso VI installed the deposed al-Qadir in Valencia as a Castilian client.
taifa-of-valencia.e: In 1092 the qadi Ibn Jahhaf killed al-Qadir and appealed to the Almoravids. Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, besieged the city and took it in June 1094, creating the Lordship of Valencia.

taifa-of-baeza.t: The breakaway realm of the Almohad prince al-Bayyasi, whose alliance with Castile hastened the fall of the upper Guadalquivir.
taifa-of-baeza.o: In 1224, amid a succession crisis in the Almohad Caliphate after the death of Yusuf II, the Almohad prince Abd Allah al-Bayyasi, a governor in al-Andalus, proclaimed himself caliph at Baeza and sought the support of Ferdinand III of Castile against his rivals.
taifa-of-baeza.r: Al-Bayyasi ruled Baeza and nearby towns as a Castilian ally and vassal, handing over castles such as Martos and Andújar in exchange for military help. This open dependence on a Christian king discredited him among Andalusi Muslims.
taifa-of-baeza.e: In 1226 al-Bayyasi was murdered by his own followers near Almodóvar while fleeing Córdoba. Baeza soon passed to Ferdinand III, among the first major towns of the Guadalquivir to fall to the Crown of Castile.

tashkent-hakimate.t: A short-lived city-state centred on Tashkent, built by Yunus Khoja on the Kazakh trade frontier before Kokand absorbed it.
tashkent-hakimate.o: In the 18th century Tashkent was divided into four quarters under rival leaders and passed under Kazakh and Dzungar overlordship. Around 1784 Yunus Khoja, hakim of one quarter, united the city and threw off the authority of the Kazakh khans of the Senior Juz.
tashkent-hakimate.r: Yunus Khoja ruled Tashkent as an independent state, extending control over nearby towns and Kazakh pastures and trading with Russia, which welcomed the caravans. He built a strong army and fought the Khanate of Kokand, defeating it in 1799 and briefly taking Khujand.
tashkent-hakimate.e: Yunus Khoja died around 1803, and his sons quarrelled. Alim Khan of the Khanate of Kokand conquered Tashkent in 1808 or 1809, after which it remained a Kokandi city until the Russian conquest of 1865.

taifa-of-badajoz.t: The great western taifa of al-Andalus, ruled by the Aftasid dynasty from Badajoz across much of what is now Extremadura and central Portugal.
taifa-of-badajoz.o: After 1009 the freedman Sabur al-Saqlabi took control of the old Lower March around Mérida and Badajoz. On his death in 1022 his vizier Abd Allah ibn al-Aftas, of Berber descent, seized power and founded the Aftasid dynasty, which soon added Lisbon, Évora and Santarém.
taifa-of-badajoz.r: The Aftasids governed the largest taifa in the west, from the Guadiana valley to the Tagus estuary. Their court was a literary centre: Muhammad al-Muzaffar compiled a vast anthology, and Umar al-Mutawakkil was a noted poet. The state fought Seville over its southern borders and lost Coimbra to Ferdinand I of León in 1064, then paid tribute to Castile.
taifa-of-badajoz.e: In 1093 al-Mutawakkil ceded Lisbon, Sintra and Santarém to Alfonso VI in return for protection. The Almoravids saw this as treason, took Badajoz in 1094 and executed him with his sons, ending the dynasty.

thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.t: Egypt's brief second period of Persian rule, from Artaxerxes III's reconquest to the arrival of Alexander the Great.
thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.o: After failed attempts in 351 BCE, the Persian king Artaxerxes III invaded Egypt in 343 BCE, defeating Nectanebo II of the Thirtieth Dynasty of Egypt at Pelusium and capturing Memphis. Egypt again became a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire, and Manetho counts the Persian kings as the Thirty-first Dynasty.
thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Greek writers describe a harsh reconquest, with temple treasures looted and city walls destroyed, though some stories, such as the killing of the Apis bull, may be propaganda. A local rebel, Khababash, briefly held power in the Delta in the late 330s BCE. The satrapy, ruled from Memphis, had to face unrest while Persia itself suffered the murders of Artaxerxes III and Arses.
thirty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.e: After the battle of Issus, the satrap Mazaces surrendered Egypt to Alexander the Great without a fight in 332 BCE, and it passed to the Macedonian Empire and later the Ptolemaic Empire.

taifa-of-algeciras.t: A Hammudid taifa on the Bay of Algeciras, controlling the crossing of the Strait of Gibraltar until Seville seized it in 1058.
taifa-of-algeciras.o: Algeciras, the main crossing point to Morocco, was a Hammudid possession. Around 1035 a branch of the family under Muhammad ibn al-Qasim made the town and its district a separate principality, while his cousins ruled the Taifa of Málaga.
taifa-of-algeciras.r: The state was small but strategic, controlling the port that linked al-Andalus with Ceuta and the Maghreb. Its rulers, like the Málaga line, used the caliphal titles of the Hammudids and relied on Berber troops. Little more is known about its administration.
taifa-of-algeciras.e: Around 1058 al-Mutadid of the Taifa of Seville besieged Algeciras and forced al-Qasim ibn Muhammad to surrender it. Algeciras was later the Almoravids' landing place in 1086.

tarhuntassa.t: Tarhuntassa, a Hittite royal city and later a rival appanage kingdom, whose rulers challenged the great kings at Hattusa.
tarhuntassa.o: Around 1280 BCE Muwatalli II moved the Hittite capital, with the gods of Hattusa, to Tarhuntassa, a city in southern Anatolia whose site is still unknown. His son Urhi-Teshub moved the court back, and Hattusili III made Tarhuntassa an appanage kingdom for Muwatalli's other son Kurunta.
tarhuntassa.r: Tarhuntassa ruled the Lower Land towards the Mediterranean as a high-ranking vassal. A treaty between Tudhaliya IV and Kurunta, on a bronze tablet found at Hattusa in 1986, defines its borders and privileges. Seals suggest Kurunta later claimed the title great king.
tarhuntassa.e: Rivalry between Tarhuntassa and Hattusa weakened the empire in its last decades. Both collapsed c. 1180 BCE; afterwards a great king Hartapu, known from inscriptions at Kızıldağ, ruled in the region.

tavastia.t: Inland Finnish province around the lakes of Häme, brought under Swedish rule by the crusade of Birger Jarl in the mid-13th century.
tavastia.o: Tavastia, or Häme, covers the lake district of southern central Finland. In the late Iron Age its people, the Tavastians, formed one of the main Finnish groups alongside the Finns proper of the south-west and the Karelians in the east. They are mentioned in Rus' chronicles as the 'Yem', against whom Novgorod campaigned from the 11th century.
tavastia.r: The Tavastians lived from slash-and-burn farming, hunting, fishing and the fur trade, which took them far into the northern wilderness. They had no single ruler; local chiefs and kin groups led society. Papal letters of the 1230s complain of Tavastians returning to paganism and attacking Christians.
tavastia.e: A Swedish expedition led by Birger Jarl, known as the Second Swedish Crusade and traditionally dated 1249, subdued Tavastia and built Häme Castle. The province became part of the Kingdom of Sweden and the Diocese of Turku, and remained so until Finland passed to Russia in 1809.

theme-of-sicily.t: Byzantine military province of Sicily, based at Syracuse, which slowly fell to Arab conquest between 827 and 965.
theme-of-sicily.o: Sicily was part of the Byzantine Empire after Justinian's reconquest in 535. In the late 7th century it was organised as a theme, a province under a military governor (strategos) at Syracuse. Emperor Constans II had resided at Syracuse from 663 until his murder there in 668.
theme-of-sicily.r: The strategos commanded the island's forces and also controlled Byzantine Calabria. Sicily was a rich source of grain and tax revenue, and the papacy owned large estates there until Leo III confiscated them in the 730s. The island became increasingly Greek-speaking and Greek in its church, receiving monks and refugees from the eastern Mediterranean.
theme-of-sicily.e: In 827 the rebel commander Euphemius invited the Aghlabids of Ifriqiya, who invaded and took Palermo in 831, Syracuse in 878 and Taormina in 902. Rometta, the last Byzantine stronghold, fell in 965, completing the Emirate of Sicily.

taifa-of-ronda.t: A Berber taifa centred on the gorge-top town of Ronda, ruled by the Banu Ifran until its annexation by the Abbadids of Seville.
taifa-of-ronda.o: Around 1015 Abu Nur Hilal ibn Abi Qurra of the Banu Ifran, a Zanata Berber clan, made himself independent in Ronda and the surrounding Serranía, first as a governor for the Hammudids and then in his own name.
taifa-of-ronda.r: Ronda's position above the Tajo gorge made it nearly impregnable, and the state controlled routes between the coast and the Guadalquivir valley. Its rulers were often at war with Seville, and court intrigue was frequent: Abu Nur was briefly overthrown and later restored. The Arab baths of Ronda date from this broad period.
taifa-of-ronda.e: In 1065 al-Mutadid of the Taifa of Seville annexed Ronda, ending Ifranid rule. The town later served the Almoravids, the Almohads and the Emirate of Granada before falling to Castile in 1485.

terra-mariana.t: Medieval Livonia, the crusader land dedicated to the Virgin Mary that covered most of modern Latvia and Estonia from the 13th century to 1561.
terra-mariana.o: Terra Mariana grew out of the Livonian crusade led by Bishop Albert of Riga. In 1207 Albert received his lands as a fief of the Holy Roman Empire, and Pope Innocent III dedicated the conquered land to the Virgin Mary, giving it its name. By 1227 the Livonians, Latgalians and Estonians had been conquered.
terra-mariana.r: Terra Mariana was never a single state but a patchwork: the Archbishopric of Riga, the bishoprics of Dorpat, Ösel-Wiek and Courland, the Livonian Order, the Danish Duchy of Estonia (1219-1346), and powerful towns such as Riga and Reval. A German-speaking elite of clergy, knights and merchants ruled Latvian, Estonian and Liv peasants, and the towns flourished in Hanseatic trade.
terra-mariana.e: The Lutheran Reformation spread in the 1520s, and the Livonian War, begun by Ivan IV of Russia in 1558, broke the region apart. In 1561 the Treaty of Vilnius dissolved the Order's state, creating the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia and the Duchy of Livonia under Poland-Lithuania, while Sweden took northern Estonia.
terra-mariana.la: Middle Low German, Latin, Latvian, Estonian

twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A one-king dynasty under Amyrtaeus of Sais, who freed Egypt from Persian rule in 404 BCE.
twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Amyrtaeus, a prince of Sais and probably a grandson of an earlier rebel of the same name, led a revolt against Achaemenid Egypt when Darius II died in 404 BCE. By about 400 BCE even the Jewish garrison at Elephantine dated its documents by his reign.
twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Very little is known of his rule. He controlled the Delta and gradually the whole country, and Persia, distracted by the revolt of Cyrus the Younger, did not try to recover Egypt.
twenty-eighth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 399 to 398 BCE Amyrtaeus was overthrown by Nepherites I of Mendes, founder of the Twenty-ninth Dynasty of Egypt; an Aramaic papyrus suggests he was executed.

taifa-of-majorca.t: The Balearic Islands as an independent taifa, a base for corsairs whose raids provoked the Pisan-Catalan crusade of 1113-1115.
taifa-of-majorca.o: The Balearics had been ruled from the Taifa of Dénia. When al-Muqtadir of the Taifa of Zaragoza annexed Dénia in 1076, the island governor Abd Allah al-Murtada declared himself independent in Madina Mayurqa, the later Palma.
taifa-of-majorca.r: The islands lived from farming, fishing and Mediterranean trade, and from corsair raids on Christian shipping and the coasts of Catalonia, Provence and Italy, which brought in captives and booty. Al-Murtada was succeeded by Mubashshir Nasir al-Dawla, a freedman who ruled until 1114.
taifa-of-majorca.e: In 1113-1115 a fleet of Pisans and Catalans under Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona sacked Ibiza and Madina Mayurqa, but withdrew. The Almoravids then occupied the islands, which later formed the base of Banu Ghaniya Majorca.

tyranny-of-pherae.t: Line of ambitious tyrants in the Thessalian city of Pherae who briefly made Thessaly a great power under Jason before falling to Philip II.
tyranny-of-pherae.o: Pherae, in south-eastern Thessaly near the port of Pagasae, rose against the old aristocratic families of Larissa and Pharsalus. Around 406 BCE Lycophron of Pherae seized power and tried to dominate all of Thessaly, defeating his rivals in 404 BCE. His successor Jason built a large mercenary army and was elected tagos, leader of the Thessalian federation, around 374 BCE.
tyranny-of-pherae.r: The tyrants depended on paid mercenaries, the port of Pagasae and alliances with outside powers. Jason planned a fleet and even, according to Xenophon, a campaign against Persia, but was assassinated in 370 BCE. Alexander of Pherae (369-358 BCE) was notorious for cruelty and fought Thebes, killing Pelopidas at Cynoscephalae in 364 BCE though losing the battle.
tyranny-of-pherae.e: Alexander was murdered by his wife Thebe and her brothers, who ruled in turn. Their struggle with the Thessalian League brought in Philip II of Macedon, who defeated the Phocian allies of Pherae at the Crocus Field in 352 BCE and expelled the tyrants. Thessaly then came under Macedonian control.

third-portuguese-republic.t: Portugal's democratic republic, born in the Carnation Revolution of 1974, which ended the empire and took the country into Europe.
third-portuguese-republic.o: On 25 April 1974 the Armed Forces Movement, junior officers weary of the colonial wars, overthrew the Estado Novo (Portugal) in the almost bloodless Carnation Revolution. A turbulent revolutionary period followed, with nationalisations and land seizures, until a moderate coup on 25 November 1975.
third-portuguese-republic.r: The Constitution of 1976 established a semi-presidential democracy. Portugal granted independence to Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Angola, Cape Verde and São Tomé in 1974-1975, receiving hundreds of thousands of returnees. Mário Soares's Socialists and the Social Democrats alternated in power. Portugal joined the European Economic Community in 1986 and adopted the euro in 1999, and handed Macau to China the same year.
third-portuguese-republic.e: Portugal remains a parliamentary democracy and member of the European Union and NATO. After the 2011 debt crisis and bailout, it recovered with growing tourism and investment.

taexali.t: People of north-east Scotland recorded by Ptolemy, who named the headland of Kinnaird Head after them and listed their town Devana.
taexali.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Taexali in the north-east of Scotland, in modern Aberdeenshire, with a headland, Taexalorum Promontorium, usually identified as Kinnaird Head, and a settlement called Devana, perhaps near the Dee or the Don. They grew from local Iron Age farming communities of the lowlands between the Dee and the Deveron.
taexali.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. The region is rich in hillforts, souterrains and recumbent stone circles from earlier ages, and Roman marching camps, such as those at Raedykes and Normandykes, show that Roman armies under Agricola and later Severus passed through their lands. Mixed farming on fertile lowland soils supported a relatively dense population.
taexali.e: The Taexali disappear from the record after Ptolemy. Their territory later formed part of the Kingdom of the Picts, whose symbol stones are especially numerous in Aberdeenshire.

trucial-states.t: The British-protected sheikhdoms of the lower Gulf coast, bound by maritime truces from 1820 and united as the UAE in 1971.
trucial-states.o: After expeditions against the Qawasim of the Sheikhdom of Ras al-Khaimah, Britain imposed the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 on the rulers of the coast. The Perpetual Maritime Truce of 1853 banned warfare at sea, giving the Trucial States, or Trucial Coast, their name, and exclusive agreements in 1892 gave Britain control of their foreign relations.
trucial-states.r: Each sheikh governed his own territory; Britain managed defence and foreign affairs through a political agent, based at Sharjah and from 1954 at Dubai. Members were Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm al-Quwain, Ras al-Khaimah, later Fujairah and briefly Kalba. A Trucial States Council from 1952 and the Trucial Oman Scouts provided common institutions, and oil from 1962 transformed Abu Dhabi.
trucial-states.e: In 1968 Britain announced its withdrawal from east of Suez. After negotiations, six sheikhdoms formed the United Arab Emirates on 2 December 1971, and Ras al-Khaimah joined in 1972.

tibetan-empire.t: The empire of the Yarlung kings that united the Tibetan plateau, rivalled Tang China for the Silk Road and brought Buddhism and writing to Tibet.
tibetan-empire.o: Clan chiefs of the Yarlung valley, led by Namri Songtsen, united much of central Tibet in the early 7th century. His son Songtsen Gampo made Lhasa his capital, absorbed Zhangzhung in the west and married princesses from Tang China and, by tradition, Nepal, establishing the empire as a major Asian power.
tibetan-empire.r: The emperor (tsenpo) ruled through powerful noble clans and ministers; a census and military districts underpinned a formidable cavalry army. Writing in a script based on Indian models is credited to Songtsen Gampo's reign. Tibet conquered the Tuyuhun in 663, contested the Tarim Basin with Tang China, briefly occupied Chang'an in 763 and held Dunhuang. Trisong Detsen made Buddhism the state religion and founded Samye monastery.
tibetan-empire.e: After the treaty with Tang of 821 to 822, recorded on a pillar in Lhasa, court conflict over Buddhism grew. The emperor Langdarma was assassinated, traditionally in 842, and a succession dispute broke the empire apart, beginning the Era of Fragmentation. Its kings and script remained foundations of Tibetan identity.

tundama.t: A Muisca lordship around modern Duitama whose ruler led the last organised resistance of the Muisca against the Spanish.
tundama.o: Tundama was a territory of the Muisca Confederation in the north of the high plateau, around modern Duitama in Boyacá. It was ruled by a chief also called Tundama and stood among the lordships independent of the zaque of the Zacazgo of Hunza.
tundama.r: Tundama was a chiefdom of farming communities growing maize, potatoes and quinoa around lakes and marshes. Its chiefs allied with neighbouring Iraca and fought both the zaque and the zipa. Little is known of its internal organisation beyond Spanish accounts of the conquest.
tundama.e: In 1539 the Spanish under Baltasar Maldonado defeated Tundama at the Battle of Bonza after fierce resistance, and the chief was later killed. Duitama became a town in the New Kingdom of Granada, and the chief is remembered as a hero of indigenous resistance.

three-leagues.t: The Alpine republic of the Grisons, a federation of three leagues of communes that ruled the Valtellina and allied with the Swiss for three centuries.
three-leagues.o: The League of God's House, the Grey League and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions formed alliances with one another during the 15th century, completed by 1471. Acting together as the Free State of the Three Leagues, they became associates of the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1497 and 1498 and fought beside the Swiss in the Swabian War of 1499.
three-leagues.r: Sovereignty lay with the communes, which voted on major decisions, an early form of direct democracy. A common diet met in rotation at Chur, Ilanz and Davos. In 1512 the leagues conquered the Valtellina, Bormio and Chiavenna, which they ruled as subject lands. The Grisons troubles of 1618 to 1639, a civil war entangled with Spanish and French interests, tore the state apart.
three-leagues.e: In 1797 the Valtellina broke away and joined Napoleon's Cisalpine Republic. In 1799 French forces attached the leagues to the Helvetic Republic, and in 1803 they became the Swiss canton of Graubünden.

titti.t: A small Celtiberian people of the Jalón valley, allies of the Belli in the war with Rome that began at Segeda in 153 BCE.
titti.o: The Titti were one of the Celtiberian peoples of the middle Ebro tributaries, probably around the Jalón valley in modern Zaragoza province. They are known almost only from Appian's account of the Celtiberian wars, which links them closely with the Belli.
titti.r: Nothing is known of their institutions beyond their dependence on the Belli. When Segeda enlarged its walls, it forced the Titti to settle there, which Rome treated as a breach of the treaty of Gracchus.
titti.e: They fought with the Belli and Arevaci in the wars of 153 to 133 BCE and are last mentioned in that conflict. After the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE their territory was absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

transcaucasian-commissariat.t: The first regional government of Transcaucasia after the October Revolution, which refused to recognise Bolshevik power and paved the way for independence.
transcaucasian-commissariat.o: After the Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd in November 1917, Georgian Mensheviks, Armenian Dashnaks and Azerbaijani Musavatists in Tiflis refused to accept their rule. On 28 November 1917 they formed the Transcaucasian Commissariat as a provisional government for the region, splitting from the Russian Republic in practice.
transcaucasian-commissariat.r: Chaired by the Georgian Menshevik Evgeni Gegechkori, it was a coalition of the three main national parties. It signed the Erzincan armistice with the Ottoman Empire in December 1917 as the Russian army melted away from the Caucasus front, and faced rising ethnic violence and food shortages. In February 1918 it convened the Transcaucasian Sejm from deputies elected to the Russian Constituent Assembly.
transcaucasian-commissariat.e: Under pressure from Ottoman advances and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the Sejm declared independence in April 1918, replacing the Commissariat with the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic. Its brief life marked the first step from Russian rule towards the separate republics of Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan.

cr.a: Russian Tzar Ministry of Internal Affairs

taifa-of-toledo.t: The central taifa of al-Andalus under the Dhul-Nunid dynasty, famous for its scientists and for its fall to Alfonso VI of Castile in 1085.
taifa-of-toledo.o: Toledo, the old Visigothic capital and frontier city of the Middle March, threw off caliphal rule around 1010. Its notables first chose local leaders, then invited the Berber Banu Dhi al-Nun, lords of Uclés and Huete, whose Ismail al-Zafir established the dynasty in the 1030s.
taifa-of-toledo.r: Al-Mamun (1043-1075) made Toledo one of the most powerful taifas, conquering Valencia in 1065 and Córdoba in 1075. His court sponsored science: the astronomer al-Zarqali produced the Toledan Tables, and Ibn Wafid laid out botanical gardens. A large Mozarab Christian and Jewish population lived in the city, and tribute was paid to León and Castile.
taifa-of-toledo.e: Al-Mamun's grandson al-Qadir, unpopular and dependent on Castile, surrendered Toledo to Alfonso VI on 25 May 1085. The loss shocked al-Andalus and led the remaining taifas to call in the Almoravids. Toledo became a centre of translation from Arabic into Latin.

tomis.t: Milesian colony on the western Black Sea coast, later famous as the place of Ovid's exile and today the Romanian port of Constanta.
tomis.o: Tomis was settled by Greeks from Miletus on a peninsula of the western Black Sea shore, in a region the Greeks called Scythia Minor, probably in the 6th century BCE. It began as a trading post beside the older colony of Histria and grew slowly into a city with its own territory, trading with the Getae and other Thracian peoples of the Dobruja hinterland.
tomis.r: Like other West Pontic colonies, Tomis was a self-governing polis with a council and assembly and close ties to its mother city Miletus. Its economy rested on grain, fish and exchange with inland peoples, whose raids were a constant threat. In the Hellenistic period it struck its own coins and joined neighbours such as Callatis and Odessos in a league of Pontic cities.
tomis.e: The Roman general Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus brought the West Pontic cities under Roman control in 72-71 BCE. The poet Ovid, exiled there by Augustus in 8 CE, complained of its cold and its barbarous neighbours. Tomis later became the capital of the Roman province of Scythia and is today Constanta.

thembu-kingdom.t: The Thembu paramountcy of the eastern Cape, a senior Nguni royal house whose descendants include Nelson Mandela.
thembu-kingdom.o: The Thembu were among the Nguni-speaking peoples settled between the Kei and Mthatha rivers, with royal genealogies reaching back many generations before written records. By the 18th century the Thembu paramount was recognised as holding senior rank among the southern Nguni, alongside the Xhosa and Mpondo royal houses.
thembu-kingdom.r: The king ruled through councils of chiefs and counsellors, with cattle as the measure of wealth and the basis of marriage alliances. Royal houses were divided into the Great House and the Right-Hand House, a pattern shared with the Xhosa Kingdom. Under Ngubengcuka in the early 19th century the Thembu sought alliances with the Cape Colony against raiders displaced by the wars of that era.
thembu-kingdom.e: Missionary influence and Cape magistrates spread through Thembuland from the mid-19th century, and after conflicts under Ngangelizwe the territory was annexed to the Cape Colony by 1885. The royal house continues, and Nelson Mandela was a descendant of Ngubengcuka.

turgesh-khaganate.t: A Turkic khaganate of the Chu and Ili valleys that led the steppe resistance to the Arab conquest of Transoxiana.
turgesh-khaganate.o: The Turgesh were one of the tribes of the On Oq confederation of the Western Turkic Khaganate. Their chief Wuzhile took Suyab around 699 as the Western Turkic state collapsed, and his son Saqal succeeded him before being killed by the Second Turkic Khaganate in 711.
turgesh-khaganate.r: Under Suluk, who rose around 716, the Turgesh became a major power, allied with the Tibetan Empire and the Sogdian princes against the Umayyads. Arab sources call him Abu Muzahim, 'the one who jostles'. He defeated an Arab army at the Battle of the Defile in 731 and the 'Day of Thirst' in 724, and sustained a court at Suyab and Talas on Sogdian trade.
turgesh-khaganate.e: Suluk was murdered in 738 after a defeat at Kharistan, and civil war between the Yellow and Black Turgesh factions followed. Tang China intervened, and by 766 the Karluk Yabgu had taken Suyab and the Turgesh lands.

tuwana.t: Tuwana, a Neo-Hittite kingdom around Tyana in southern Cappadocia, whose king Warpalawa is carved on the Ivriz rock relief.
tuwana.o: Tuwana lay in the plain south of modern Niğde, in the region the Assyrians called Tabal. It emerged as a separate kingdom in the 8th century BCE around the old city of Tuwanuwa, later Greek Tyana.
tuwana.r: King Warpalawa ruled with Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions and is shown on the rock relief at Ivriz before the storm god Tarhunza, who holds grapes and ears of wheat, symbols of the land's fertility. He paid tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III of the Assyrian Empire in 738 BCE.
tuwana.e: After Warpalawa, Tuwana fades from the record during the rise of Phrygia and the Cimmerian invasions of the 7th century BCE. Tyana remained an important city in Cappadocia.

taifa-of-tavira.t: A brief independent lordship at Tavira in the eastern Algarve, one of the many local regimes of the 1140s revolt against the Almoravids.
taifa-of-tavira.o: In 1145, as the Muridun revolt led by Ibn Qasi spread through the Algarve and Almoravid authority collapsed, local leaders took control of Tavira, a port on the Gilão river, and held it independently.
taifa-of-tavira.r: Known only from brief mentions in Arabic chronicles, the state consisted of the town and its coastal district, with fishing, salt and trade along the Algarve coast. Its rulers were drawn into the shifting alliances among the Second Taifa of Mértola, the Second Taifa of Silves and the Taifa of Beja and Évora.
taifa-of-tavira.e: Around 1150 Tavira accepted Almohad rule along with the rest of the western Algarve. It was conquered by the Kingdom of Portugal in 1242.

taifa-of-tortosa.t: A taifa at the mouth of the Ebro ruled by former Slavic palace officials, prized for its port and shipyards before Zaragoza swallowed it.
taifa-of-tortosa.o: When the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed in civil war after 1009, the saqaliba (freedmen of European origin) of the Amirid household seized several eastern towns. At Tortosa the freedman Labib al-Amiri took power, for a time also holding Valencia in partnership with Mubarak and Muzaffar.
taifa-of-tortosa.r: Tortosa lived from the Ebro trade, timber from its hinterland and the shipyards that had built caliphal fleets. Its rulers, all freedmen, lacked dynastic legitimacy and leaned on stronger neighbours such as Dénia and Zaragoza, and on payments to the Counts of Barcelona. Successive governors included Muqatil, Yali and Nabil.
taifa-of-tortosa.e: Around 1060 the Hudid ruler al-Muqtadir of Zaragoza annexed Tortosa, ending its independence. The city stayed Muslim until Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona took it in 1148, after which it became a key port of Catalonia.

tunjur-kingdom.t: A mysterious kingdom that ruled Darfur and Wadai before the Keira sultans, remembered through traditions and the ruins of Ain Farah.
tunjur-kingdom.o: The origins of the Tunjur are obscure and debated: traditions variously claim Arab, Nubian or local descent. By around 1400 they had replaced the earlier Daju kingdom as the dominant power in the Jebel Marra and northern Darfur region, and their rule extended west into what became Wadai.
tunjur-kingdom.r: Almost nothing is documented about Tunjur government. The red-brick ruins of Ain Farah, including what may be a mosque and earlier church-like structures, are attributed to them, suggesting links with the Nile valley. They are traditionally credited with introducing Islam to Darfur and controlling caravan trade between the Nile and the Chad basin.
tunjur-kingdom.e: In the 17th century Tunjur rule was overthrown in Wadai by Abd al-Karim, founder of the Wadai Empire, and in Darfur by the Keira dynasty of the Darfur Sultanate. The Tunjur survived as a people in Darfur and Chad.

trapezus.t: Trapezus, a Greek colony on the south-eastern Black Sea coast that became Trebizond, where Xenophon's Ten Thousand reached the sea.
trapezus.o: Colonists from Sinope founded Trapezus on a table-shaped headland, from which its name comes, traditionally in 756 BCE. It controlled a harbour and the route inland to the Armenian highlands, among the Colchian and Pontic peoples of the coast.
trapezus.r: Trapezus was a Greek city governed by its citizens, paying tribute to Sinope and later recognising Persian overlordship. In 400 BCE the Ten Thousand Greek mercenaries described by Xenophon arrived here after their march, and the city hosted them for a month. It traded timber, metals and hazelnuts.
trapezus.e: Trapezus was absorbed by the Kingdom of Pontus in the 2nd century BCE and passed to the Roman world after Pompey defeated Mithridates VI in 63 BCE. It later became Trebizond, capital of the Empire of Trebizond.

texuandri.t: People of the sandy heathlands of the Kempen and Brabant whose land, Toxandria, became the first Roman foothold of the Salian Franks.
texuandri.o: Known chiefly from Pliny, who lists them among the peoples of Gallia Belgica, the Texuandri lived in the region between the Meuse and the Scheldt, in the modern Belgian Kempen and Dutch North Brabant. They may have been a subdivision of the Tungri.
texuandri.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their land was thinly settled, with scattered farms on poor sandy soils, and inscriptions record Texuandrian soldiers serving in the Roman army, including in Britain.
texuandri.e: In the 3rd and 4th centuries the area was disrupted by Frankish raids. In 358 the future emperor Julian allowed the Salian Franks to settle in Toxandria as Roman allies, and the region became the cradle of Frankish power in the Low Countries.

thebes.t: Leading city of Boeotia whose generals Epaminondas and Pelopidas broke Spartan power at Leuctra in 371 BCE and briefly made Thebes the first power of Greece.
thebes.o: Thebes grew from the Mycenaean palace town on the Kadmeia, surviving the collapse c. 1200 BCE. In the Archaic period it became the chief city of Boeotia and, from the late 6th century BCE, the head of the Boeotian League, competing with Orchomenus and Plataea for leadership.
thebes.r: Thebes was ruled mostly by landowning oligarchies. It sided with Persia in 480 BCE and was punished after Plataea, then backed Sparta in the Peloponnesian War. Sparta seized the Kadmeia in 382 BCE, but Pelopidas liberated it in 379 BCE. With the Sacred Band and Epaminondas's deep phalanx, Thebes won at Leuctra, freed Messenia and founded Megalopolis.
thebes.e: After Epaminondas died at Mantinea in 362 BCE, Theban power faded. Defeated with Athens at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, Thebes revolted and was razed by Alexander in 335 BCE. Cassander rebuilt it in 316 BCE, and it passed under Rome in 146 BCE.

tabal.t: Tabal, a group of Neo-Hittite kingdoms on the central Anatolian plateau, caught between Assyria, Phrygia and Urartu.
tabal.o: Tabal emerged after the Hittite collapse in the region of later Cappadocia, south of the Kızılırmak. From the 9th century BCE Assyrian texts mention the kings of Tabal, sometimes as many as twenty, but at times one ruler dominated, such as Tuwati and his son Wasusarma.
tabal.r: Its rulers wrote Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions, often styling themselves great king, and drew wealth from silver mines and the trade routes of the plateau. The Assyrians demanded tribute and tried to secure loyalty through marriage alliances with local kings.
tabal.e: Sargon II gave his daughter to Ambaris of Bit-Burutash, but deposed him in 713 BCE for plotting with Phrygia and Urartu. Tabal was later overrun by Cimmerian invaders in the 7th century BCE and disappears around 650 BCE.

tauromenium.t: Greek city on a terrace above the Ionian Sea, founded by survivors of Naxos, famous for its theatre with a view of Etna.
tauromenium.o: After Dionysius I destroyed Naxos in 403 BCE, its survivors and Sicels settled on Monte Tauro above the old site. In 358 BCE Andromachus, father of the historian Timaeus, refounded the community as a Greek city, Tauromenium.
tauromenium.r: Under Andromachus the city welcomed Timoleon when he landed in Sicily in 344 BCE to free Syracuse. Tauromenium later passed under Agathocles and then Hieron II of Syracuse. Its theatre, built in the Hellenistic period and enlarged by the Romans, overlooks the coast and Mount Etna. Inscriptions record its magistrates and public finances in detail.
tauromenium.e: When Rome captured Syracuse in 212 BCE, Tauromenium came under Roman rule, enjoying the privileged status of an allied city. Octavian later made it a colony after it sided with Sextus Pompeius. It survives as Taormina.

third-republic-of-venezuela.t: The patriot republic Bolívar rebuilt from Angostura on the Orinoco, which launched the campaigns that freed northern South America.
third-republic-of-venezuela.o: After exile in Jamaica and Haiti, Bolívar returned to Venezuela in 1816. In 1817 patriot forces under Manuel Piar and Bolívar captured the Guayana region and its town of Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar, on the Orinoco, giving the patriots a secure base. The republic was proclaimed there.
third-republic-of-venezuela.r: Bolívar consolidated his authority, ordering Piar's execution in 1817 for insubordination. José Antonio Páez won over the llaneros of the plains, and British and Irish volunteers formed the British Legion. The newspaper Correo del Orinoco spread patriot views from 1818. The Congress of Angostura met in February 1819, when Bolívar delivered his famous address on government.
third-republic-of-venezuela.e: After Bolívar's crossing of the Andes and victory at Boyacá in August 1819, the Congress of Angostura proclaimed the union of Venezuela and New Granada as Gran Colombia in December 1819.

taurida-soviet-socialist-republic.t: A Bolshevik republic in the Crimea in spring 1918, ended within weeks by a German advance and a Crimean Tatar revolt.
taurida-soviet-socialist-republic.o: After the Bolsheviks crushed the Crimean People's Republic in January 1918, they proclaimed the Soviet Socialist Republic of Taurida in March 1918 at Simferopol, covering the Crimea and the neighbouring mainland districts. Anton Slutsky became chairman of its council of people's commissars.
taurida-soviet-socialist-republic.r: The republic was dominated by Bolsheviks and radical sailors from Sevastopol, and its brief rule was marked by requisitions and mass killings of officers and property owners. It nationalised land and property but had little real administration, and it faced hostility from the Crimean Tatars.
taurida-soviet-socialist-republic.e: In April 1918 German troops entered the Crimea, and Crimean Tatars rose in revolt. Slutsky and other leaders were captured near Alushta and shot. The Germans then set up the Crimean Regional Government.

taifa-of-crevillent.t: A small Muslim lordship near Elche whose ra'is ruled under Christian overlords for some 75 years after the fall of Murcia.
taifa-of-crevillent.o: Around 1243, when the Third Taifa of Murcia accepted Castilian overlordship by the Treaty of Alcaraz, the Banu Hudayr family kept control of Crevillent and its district as autonomous Muslim lords, or ra'is.
taifa-of-crevillent.r: Known only from scattered documents, the lordship was a Muslim enclave of irrigated farmland under Christian protection, first of the Crown of Castile and, after the Treaty of Torrellas of 1304, of the Crown of Aragon. It survived the Mudéjar revolt of 1264-1266 and kept contacts with the Emirate of Granada.
taifa-of-crevillent.e: Around 1318 the last ra'is left for Granada, and Crevillent was absorbed into the Kingdom of Valencia. Its Muslim population remained as Mudéjares until the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609.

third-taifa-of-malaga.t: Málaga under its qadi Ibn Hassun, who ruled the city independently after the Almoravid collapse until the Almohads forced him out.
third-taifa-of-malaga.o: In 1145, as Andalusi cities expelled their Almoravid garrisons, the people of Málaga accepted the authority of their qadi, Abu al-Hakam ibn Hassun, a member of a local family of jurists.
third-taifa-of-malaga.r: Like other qadis of the second taifa period, Ibn Hassun ruled on the strength of his religious office and local support. He governed a prosperous port, but had little military power and faced pressure from Almoravid loyalists, from the Taifa of Jaén and from the advancing Almohads.
third-taifa-of-malaga.e: In 1153 the Almohads took Málaga, and Ibn Hassun is reported to have killed himself rather than be captured. The city remained under Almohad and then Nasrid rule until 1487.

talysh-khanate.t: A Caspian khanate in the subtropical lowlands and forests of Talysh, divided between Russia and Persia in 1828.
talysh-khanate.o: Around 1747, after Nader Shah's death, Jamal al-Din Khan, called Qara Khan, made the Talysh district an independent khanate, with its capital first at Astara and then Lankaran on the Caspian shore. His family claimed descent from the Safavids. The district had earlier been governed for the shahs by local Talysh chiefs.
talysh-khanate.r: The khans ruled Talysh-speaking and Azerbaijani villages in fertile lowlands and forested mountains, producing rice, silk and fish for Caspian trade. Their small state survived by balancing the Quba Khanate, Qajar Iran and Russia. Mir Mustafa Khan, who ruled from 1786, sought Russian protection against the Qajars.
talysh-khanate.e: Russian forces stormed Lankaran in 1812, and the Treaty of Gulistan in 1813 confirmed Russian protection. After Persian reoccupation in 1826, the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828 split Talysh along the Astara river, and the Russian Empire annexed the northern part.

tairona.t: Chiefdoms of Colombia's Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta that built stone-terraced towns such as the Ciudad Perdida and whose descendants still live in the mountains.
tairona.o: Settlement in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta and its Caribbean coast developed from around 200 CE, and the Tairona style, with stone architecture, emerged by about 1000 CE. Communities built towns on mountain ridges with terraces, stairways and paved paths.
tairona.r: The Tairona were organised in independent chiefdoms and towns linked by alliances, with priests called mamas holding great authority. Teyuna, known as the Ciudad Perdida or Lost City, had some 170 stone terraces and a network of paved roads. Farming of maize, cassava and fruit on terraces sustained dense populations. Their goldsmiths made fine pendants and nose ornaments in tumbaga, a gold-copper alloy.
tairona.e: Spanish contact began after the foundation of Santa Marta in 1525. The Tairona resisted for decades until a major revolt was crushed around 1600, after which towns such as Teyuna were abandoned. Their descendants, the Kogi, Arhuaco, Wiwa and Kankuamo peoples, still live in the Sierra.

thera.t: Dorian island city on volcanic Santorini, best known as the founder of Cyrene in Libya and for some of the earliest Greek inscriptions.
thera.o: After the Bronze Age eruption destroyed the Minoan town of Akrotiri, Santorini was resettled by Dorians from Laconia in the early Iron Age, led by tradition by Theras. Their town grew on the ridge of Mesa Vouno, on the south-east of the island.
thera.r: Thera was an aristocratic community with Spartan customs, and its rock-cut inscriptions of the 7th century BCE are among the oldest Greek writing. On Delphi's advice, Therans sent settlers under Battus to found Cyrene in Libya c. 631 BCE, as recorded in a later foundation decree. The island paid tribute to Athens in the Delian League from the 420s BCE.
thera.e: In the 3rd century BCE Thera became a Ptolemaic naval base, with a garrison and gymnasium. It passed under Roman control by 146 BCE, and its ancient city on Mesa Vouno remained inhabited into Byzantine times.
thera.re: Greek religion; cult of Apollo Karneios

taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve.t: A small taifa at Santa María, today's Faro, ruled by the Arab Banu Harun in the far south of present-day Portugal.
taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve.o: Around 1018 Said ibn Harun, of a local Arab family, made himself independent in the coastal town of Santa María de Harun, the later Faro, and its district in the eastern Algarve as caliphal authority disappeared.
taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve.r: The state was a small coastal principality of fishing, salt pans and dry farming, with figs, almonds and olives. Its rulers recognised the Hammudid caliphs for a time and later sought to balance between the Taifa of Silves and Seville. Little else is recorded about its government.
taifa-of-santa-maria-del-algarve.e: Around 1051 the last ruler, Muhammad ibn Said, surrendered his town to al-Mutadid of the Taifa of Seville. The town's name later gave rise to Faro, and the Algarve fell to Portugal in 1249.

taurini.t: Alpine people of the upper Po whose chief town Hannibal stormed in 218 BCE and whose name lives on in Turin.
taurini.o: The Taurini lived at the foot of the western Alps where the Dora Riparia meets the Po. Ancient writers called them Ligurian or Celtic; they were probably a Ligurian people with strong Celtic influence. Little is known of their early history.
taurini.r: They are known only from Greek and Roman writers. Their chief town, called Taurasia by Appian, controlled routes from the Alpine passes into the Po plain. In 218 BCE they were at war with the Insubres.
taurini.e: After crossing the Alps in 218 BCE, Hannibal took Taurasia in three days when its people refused his alliance, and massacred the defenders. The region later came under Rome, and Augustus founded the colony of Augusta Taurinorum on or near the site, the origin of Turin.

tarquinii.t: Etruscan city famed for its painted tombs and remembered by Rome as the home of the Tarquin dynasty.
tarquinii.o: Tarquinii, Etruscan Tarchna, grew on a plateau above the Marta valley near the coast, one of the earliest and largest Villanovan centres of Etruria. In legend it was founded by Tarchon, and the haruspex Tages, who revealed Etruscan religious lore, appeared in its fields. Its port at Gravisca welcomed Greek traders from the 6th century BCE.
tarquinii.r: Aristocratic families dominated the city and are commemorated in the painted chamber tombs of the Monterozzi necropolis, more than 200 of them, showing banquets, dancers, athletes and later underworld scenes. Its magistrates bore the title zilath, and the Spurinna family's elogia record their deeds. Roman tradition said Demaratus of Corinth settled here and his son became Rome's king Tarquinius Priscus.
tarquinii.e: Tarquinii fought Rome in the 4th century BCE, notoriously sacrificing 307 Roman prisoners in 358 BCE. After further wars it made peace and became a Roman ally around 281 BCE, and later a municipium. Its painted tombs are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

tsardom-of-russia.t: Russia under its first tsars, from Ivan the Terrible to Peter the Great, which expanded from the Volga to the Pacific.
tsardom-of-russia.o: In January 1547 Ivan IV, grand prince of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, was crowned tsar, a title derived from Caesar that claimed equality with emperors. He conquered the Khanate of Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556, opening the Volga to Russian control.
tsardom-of-russia.r: The tsar ruled as an autocrat with the boyar council, the Orthodox Church and a growing service nobility. Ivan's reign brought the Livonian War and the terror of the oprichnina. After the Rurikid line died out in 1598 the Time of Troubles followed, with Polish troops in Moscow, until Michael Romanov was elected in 1613. The law code of 1649 bound peasants as serfs, and explorers reached the Pacific by 1639.
tsardom-of-russia.e: Peter I modernised the army and state, founded Saint Petersburg in 1703 and defeated Sweden in the Great Northern War. After the Treaty of Nystad in 1721 he took the title of emperor, and the tsardom became the Russian Empire.

theodosia.t: Milesian port in south-eastern Crimea that exported grain until it was conquered by the Bosporan Kingdom in the 4th century BCE.
theodosia.o: Theodosia was founded by settlers from Miletus in the 6th century BCE on a bay of the south-eastern Crimean coast, at modern Feodosia. Its good harbour and fertile hinterland made it an important outlet for grain grown by local peoples.
theodosia.r: Theodosia lived from exporting grain, fish and hides to the Aegean, especially Athens. It long resisted absorption by the neighbouring Bosporan Kingdom, with help from Heraclea Pontica. The Bosporan ruler Satyrus I died while besieging it in 389 BCE.
theodosia.e: Leucon I of the Bosporan Kingdom captured Theodosia, probably c. 355 BCE, and developed its harbour for the grain trade with Athens. It remained a Bosporan city and centuries later became the Genoese port of Kaffa.

templar-cyprus.t: Brief rule of Cyprus by the Knights Templar after they bought the island from Richard the Lionheart, ended by a Cypriot revolt within a year.
templar-cyprus.o: Having conquered Cyprus from Isaac Komnenos in 1191, Richard I had no use for governing it during the Third Crusade. He sold the island to the Knights Templar, then led by Grand Master Robert de Sable, for 100,000 bezants, of which 40,000 were paid in advance.
templar-cyprus.r: The order sent only a small force, said to number about twenty knights and some soldiers, under Armand Bouchart to govern from Nicosia. They raised heavy taxes to pay the purchase price, and their harsh rule quickly angered the Greek population, who had already suffered under Isaac.
templar-cyprus.e: At Easter 1192 the Cypriots rose and besieged the Templars in Nicosia. The knights broke out, killing many townspeople, but realised they could not hold the island. They returned it to Richard, who sold it to Guy of Lusignan, founder of the Kingdom of Cyprus.

taifa-of-cordoba.t: The former caliphal capital governed as a council-led republic by the Jahwarid family after the caliphate was formally abolished in 1031.
taifa-of-cordoba.o: In 1031 the notables of Córdoba, exhausted by two decades of civil war, deposed the last Umayyad caliph, Hisham III, and abolished the Caliphate of Córdoba. The vizier Abu al-Hazm ibn Jahwar became head of a government that ruled through a council of leading citizens.
taifa-of-cordoba.r: The Jahwarids presented themselves as administrators rather than kings. Abu al-Hazm restored order and finances, avoided wars and maintained the city's markets and scholarship, though Córdoba had lost much of its population and grandeur. The poet Ibn Zaydun served the regime before falling out with it.
taifa-of-cordoba.e: Abd al-Malik ibn Jahwar's rule ended when al-Mutamid of the Taifa of Seville took Córdoba in 1070. Toledo held it briefly in 1075 before Seville recovered it. The city later rose again as the Second Taifa of Córdoba.

tartessos.t: A legendary kingdom of the lower Guadalquivir whose silver wealth drew Phoenician and Greek traders, remembered by Herodotus and the Bible.
tartessos.o: Tartessos emerged in the 9th century BCE in the region of Huelva, Seville and Cádiz, where a local Late Bronze Age society came into intense contact with Phoenician traders from Gadir. The silver and copper of the Río Tinto mines fuelled the exchange, and Greek and Biblical sources (as Tarshish) remembered it as a land of fabulous wealth.
tartessos.r: Archaeology shows an elite culture that adopted eastern goods and styles, seen in the gold of the El Carambolo treasure and the palace-sanctuary of Cancho Roano. Herodotus tells of King Arganthonios, who ruled for decades and welcomed Phocaean Greeks around 600 BCE. Whether Tartessos was a unified kingdom or a network of chiefdoms is still debated, as is its link to the south-western script.
tartessos.e: Around 500 BCE the Tartessian culture declined, perhaps through falling silver demand, the eclipse of Tyre and the rise of Carthage. Its lands passed to the Turdetani, whom Strabo saw as its heirs, and the name Tartessos became a byword for lost riches.

treveri.t: Powerful people of the Moselle, famed for their cavalry, whose land became the site of Trier, a Roman imperial capital.
treveri.o: The Treveri lived along the Moselle in modern Luxembourg and Rhineland-Palatinate. They were counted among the Belgae, though Tacitus says they claimed Germanic descent. Their great oppidum on the Titelberg in Luxembourg was a centre of minting and trade.
treveri.r: Caesar calls their cavalry the best in Gaul. Their nobility split between Indutiomarus, leader of the anti-Roman party, and his son-in-law Cingetorix, who backed Caesar.
treveri.e: Indutiomarus led a revolt in 54 BCE and was killed; Labienus defeated the Treveri in 53 BCE. Around 16 BCE the Romans founded Augusta Treverorum (Trier), which became the capital of the Gallic Empire and of the western Roman Empire under Constantine.

taifa-of-carmona.t: A Berber taifa ruled by the Banu Birzal from the fortress town of Carmona, a rival of Seville in the lower Guadalquivir valley.
taifa-of-carmona.o: The Banu Birzal, Zanata Berbers brought to al-Andalus as soldiers by al-Mansur, took control of Carmona around 1013 during the civil war that destroyed the Caliphate of Córdoba. Their leader Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Birzali made the town the base of an independent principality.
taifa-of-carmona.r: Carmona, with strong Roman walls on a ridge above the fertile Vega, was one of the most defensible towns of the region. Its rulers at times also held Écija and Almodóvar and allied with the Hammudids of Málaga against Seville. The state was a military lordship rather than a court of letters.
taifa-of-carmona.e: After long wars, al-Mutadid of the Taifa of Seville took Carmona in 1067, and the Birzalid family was eclipsed. Ferdinand III of Castile captured the town in 1247.

tabasaran-maysumate.t: A small principality of the Tabasaran people in southern Dagestan, in the mountains behind Derbent, ruled by hereditary maysums.
tabasaran-maysumate.o: Tabasaran, a mountainous district west of Derbent, was home to the Tabasaran people, Muslims since the early Islamic centuries. By the 16th century a hereditary ruler with the title maysum governed part of it from Khuchni, while another part was ruled by a qadi; the origins of the dynasty are obscure.
tabasaran-maysumate.r: The maysums ruled villages of farmers and herders through local nobles and customary law, and the district was known for its carpets. Tabasaran was a vassal of the Safavid Empire for much of this period and was drawn into the struggles between the khans of Derbent and Quba, the Ottomans and Russia.
tabasaran-maysumate.e: The Russian Empire established a protectorate in 1806 and annexed Tabasaran in 1813, recognised in the Treaty of Gulistan with Persia. Its lands were later absorbed into Russian administrative districts of Dagestan.

tsardom-of-vidin.t: Western Bulgarian realm of Ivan Sratsimir on the Danube, which split from Tarnovo in 1356 and was the last Bulgarian state to fall to the Ottomans.
tsardom-of-vidin.o: Tsar Ivan Alexander of the Second Bulgarian Empire made his younger son Ivan Shishman heir and gave his eldest, Ivan Sratsimir, the north-western region around Vidin. By 1356 Sratsimir ruled there as a separate tsar, and the two Bulgarian realms became rivals.
tsardom-of-vidin.r: Sratsimir ruled from Vidin's Baba Vida fortress over lands along the Danube, minting his own coins and placing his church under the Patriarch of Constantinople rather than Tarnovo. In 1365 Louis I of Hungary seized Vidin and held it for four years, trying to convert the population to Catholicism, until Wallachian and Bulgarian forces restored Sratsimir. Afterwards he became an Ottoman vassal.
tsardom-of-vidin.e: In 1396 Sratsimir opened Vidin to the crusaders of Sigismund of Hungary. After their defeat at Nicopolis, Sultan Bayezid I took Vidin and Sratsimir was captured, ending Bulgarian independence until 1878.

taifa-of-arcos.t: A small Berber-ruled taifa centred on the clifftop town of Arcos de la Frontera, one of several absorbed by the expanding Abbadids of Seville.
taifa-of-arcos.o: During the fitna after 1009, Berber troops who had served the caliphs settled in the hill towns of western al-Andalus. Around 1011 the Banu Khizrun, a Zanata Berber family, made Arcos their seat and ruled it as an independent principality.
taifa-of-arcos.r: Arcos was a fortified town controlling the Guadalete valley and routes between Seville, Jerez and the Strait. Like the other small Berber taifas of the region, it relied on its walls and on alliances with the Hammudids and the Taifa of Ronda against Seville. Only the outline of its rulers' succession is known.
taifa-of-arcos.e: The Abbadid ruler al-Mutadid of the Taifa of Seville annexed Arcos in the 1050s or 1060s as he swept up the Berber principalities of the south-west. Castile took the town in the 13th century.

tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea.t: Herod Antipas's tetrarchy in Galilee and east of the Jordan, the political setting of the ministries of John the Baptist and Jesus.
tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea.o: After the death of Herod the Great in 4 BCE, Augustus gave his son Herod Antipas two separate territories: Galilee, west of the Sea of Galilee, and Peraea, a strip east of the Jordan. Antipas first rebuilt Sepphoris, wrecked in the unrest after his father's death, as his seat.
tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea.r: Antipas ruled as a Roman client and largely respected Jewish sensibilities, minting coins without images. Around 19 CE he founded Tiberias on the lake shore, named after the emperor, and moved his capital there. The Gospels and Josephus record that he imprisoned and executed John the Baptist, and Luke says Jesus was sent to him during his trial. Fishing, farming and olive oil sustained the economy.
tetrarchy-of-galilee-and-peraea.e: His divorce of a daughter of the Nabataean king Aretas IV to marry Herodias led to a war he lost in 36. Accused of conspiracy by his nephew Agrippa, he was deposed by Caligula in 39 and exiled to Gaul. His lands passed to the Kingdom of Herod Agrippa.

tahirid-sultanate.t: The last Sunni dynasty of medieval Yemen, successors of the Rasulids, swept away by the Mamluk and Ottoman invasions.
tahirid-sultanate.o: The Banu Tahir were a family from the Rada'a and Juban region who served the Rasulid dynasty. As Rasulid rule collapsed in the 1440s, the brothers Ali and Amir ibn Tahir seized Aden and Zabid and by 1454 had made themselves sultans of lowland and southern Yemen.
tahirid-sultanate.r: The Tahirids ruled from Rada'a, Juban, Ta'izz and Zabid and inherited the Rasulid tax system and Aden's trade, though with less wealth. They were Sunni patrons of learning; Sultan Amir ibn Abd al-Wahhab built the Amiriya Madrasa at Rada'a, completed in 1504, with exceptional painted interiors. They fought the Zaydi imams for the highlands and Sanaa.
tahirid-sultanate.e: In 1515 a Mamluk Sultanate fleet arrived to fight the Portuguese and turned on the Tahirids. Amir was killed in 1517, the year the Mamluks fell to the Ottoman Empire. Remnants held out in Aden until 1538, when Yemen Eyalet began.

torks.t: Oghuz Turkic nomads of the southern Russian steppe who fought the Rus' and later served them as frontier guards.
torks.o: The Torks were Oghuz Turks who moved west from the Aral and Caspian steppes in the late 10th century, part of the westward migrations that followed the collapse of the Oghuz Yabgu State. Byzantine writers called them Uzes. In 985 they appear as allies of Prince Vladimir of Kiev in his campaign against the Volga Bulgars.
torks.r: The Torks were pastoral nomads organised in clans under chiefs, with no strong central power. They competed with the Pechenegs for the steppe north of the Black Sea and raided both Rus' and the Byzantine Balkans; a large Uz horde crossed the Danube in 1064 before being destroyed by disease and Bulgarian attacks.
torks.e: In 1060 a combined Rus' army defeated the Torks, and the arrival of the Cumans soon after forced them from the steppe. Many settled as allies of the Kievan princes along the Ros River, among the Chorni Klobuky, 'Black Hats', who guarded the frontier.

taifa-of-niebla.t: A taifa based on the walled town of Niebla on the Tinto river, ruled by the Arab Banu Yahya until Seville annexed it.
taifa-of-niebla.o: Around 1023 Ahmad ibn Yahya al-Yahsubi, of an Arab family long settled in the region, established an independent principality around Niebla, taking advantage of the weakness of the Hammudid caliphs and the rivalries of the south-western taifas.
taifa-of-niebla.r: Niebla controlled the lower Tinto valley and the mining district inland, with its red stone walls and fertile riverland. Its rulers, styled with honorifics such as Izz al-Dawla, were caught between the Taifa of Seville and the Taifa of Huelva, and briefly accepted Seville's protection before resisting it.
taifa-of-niebla.e: In 1053 al-Mutadid of the Taifa of Seville annexed Niebla, deposing Muhammad ibn Yahya. The town later reappeared twice as an independent taifa, in the Second Taifa of Niebla and the Third Taifa of Niebla.

tudmir.t: The autonomous Christian principality of Theodemir in Murcia and Alicante, whose 713 surrender treaty is one of the earliest documents of al-Andalus.
tudmir.o: Theodemir, a Visigothic noble who governed the south-east, resisted the Muslim invaders and then negotiated. In April 713 he signed a treaty with Abd al-Aziz ibn Musa, keeping control of seven towns, including Orihuela, Mula, Lorca and Alicante, in return for submission and tribute.
tudmir.r: The treaty guaranteed the Christians their lives, property and churches as long as they paid an annual tax in coin and in kind, wheat, barley, vinegar, honey and oil, and did not shelter enemies. Theodemir ruled as a client prince, and the region became known in Arabic as Tudmir after him. His successor Athanagild kept the autonomy for a time.
tudmir.e: Arab settlers, especially Syrian troops after 743, moved into the region, eroding Christian autonomy. By the reign of Abd al-Rahman I it was absorbed into the Emirate of Córdoba, and in 831 Abd al-Rahman II founded Murcia as the capital of the province of Tudmir.

turmodigi.t: A people of the upper Arlanzón in Burgos, whose town Segisamo served as Augustus' base in the Cantabrian Wars.
turmodigi.o: The Turmodigi, or Murbogi, lived around the upper Arlanzón and Pisuerga in modern Burgos province from the later Iron Age, between the Vaccaei, Autrigones and Cantabri. Their language was probably Celtic.
turmodigi.r: Little is known of their society. Their main settlement was Segisamo, modern Sasamón, and they farmed the northern Meseta and herded in its uplands.
turmodigi.e: In 26 BCE Augustus made Segisamo his camp for the campaign against the Cantabri, and the Turmodigi were integrated into Hispania Tarraconensis. Segisamo continued as a Roman town.

taifa-of-molina.t: An obscure frontier lordship at Molina de Aragón, ruled by the Banu Galbun, whose lord appears as El Cid's friend Abengalbón in the Cantar de mio Cid.
taifa-of-molina.o: The Banu Galbun appear to have taken control of the castle of Molina and its district in the upper Gallo valley around 1012, as the Middle March of al-Andalus fragmented after the fall of the Caliphate of Córdoba. Little more is known of its beginnings.
taifa-of-molina.r: Molina was a small border principality between the taifas of Toledo, Zaragoza and Albarracín, more a fortified lordship than a full kingdom. It is known mainly from Christian sources and from the epic Cantar de mio Cid, in which its lord Abengalbón is a loyal ally who hosts the Cid's wife and daughters.
taifa-of-molina.e: Molina came under Almoravid control around 1100. In about 1129 Alfonso I of Aragon took the town, and it was soon granted to the Lara family, becoming the Lordship of Molina.

turaida.t: Livonian chiefdom on the lower Gauja, whose leader Caupo became the crusaders' most important native ally and visited the pope in Rome.
turaida.o: Turaida, Thoreida in Latin, was a land of the Livonians, a Finnic people, on the lower course of the Gauja river in modern Latvia. Its fortified hill at Turaida controlled river traffic and was the seat of the elder Caupo at the beginning of the 13th century.
turaida.r: The Livs farmed, fished and traded along the Gauja and Daugava. Caupo accepted baptism early, travelled to Rome around 1203 and met Pope Innocent III, and supported Bishop Albert of Riga against his own countrymen, who rose against him in 1212. The Livs of Turaida supplied troops to the crusaders' campaigns in Estonia.
turaida.e: Caupo was killed at the Battle of St Matthew's Day in 1217. Turaida came under the bishop of Riga, who built a stone castle there in 1214, and it became part of the Archbishopric of Riga. The Livonian language slowly gave way to Latvian.

turkmen-ssr.t: The Soviet republic of the Turkmen, a desert land of gas fields and cotton built around the Karakum Canal.
turkmen-ssr.o: The Turkmen SSR was created in October 1924 in the national delimitation of Soviet Central Asia, from the Transcaspian region of the Turkestan ASSR and Turkmen districts of the Bukharan and Khorezm republics. Its capital was Poltoratsk, renamed Ashgabat in 1927.
turkmen-ssr.r: Soviet rule settled nomadic and semi-nomadic Turkmen tribes, collectivised farming and fought Basmachi resistance led by Junaid Khan into the 1930s. In 1948 an earthquake destroyed Ashgabat, killing tens of thousands. The Karakum Canal, begun in the 1950s, carried water from the Amu Darya for cotton, and natural gas became a major export.
turkmen-ssr.e: Saparmurat Niyazov, first secretary from 1985, led the republic to independence on 27 October 1991, when it became Turkmenistan.

tsongkha.t: A Tibetan kingdom in Amdo, centred on modern Xining, that allied with the Song against the Tanguts and controlled a southern branch of the Silk Road.
tsongkha.o: After the Tibetan Empire fragmented, Tibetan tribes in the Huangshui valley of Amdo brought in Gusiluo, a youth claiming descent from the old royal line, around 1008. After years as a figurehead of local strongmen he established his own court at Qingtang (modern Xining) around 1032.
tsongkha.r: Gusiluo was a Buddhist ruler presiding over a loose federation of Tibetan clans. He allied with the Song Dynasty, which gave him titles and subsidies, and defeated Tangut attacks from Western Xia in the 1030s. When Tangut wars disrupted the Hexi Corridor, caravans used the Qinghai route through his territory, and Qingtang grew rich on trade in horses and other goods.
tsongkha.e: After Gusiluo's death in 1065 the kingdom was divided among his descendants and weakened by feuds. The Song annexed the region in campaigns of 1099 and 1104, though Song control was soon lost to the Jin dynasty (1115-1234) and Western Xia.

theme-of-longobardia.t: Byzantine province of southern Italy, governed from Bari, created after the empire recovered Apulia in the late 9th century.
theme-of-longobardia.o: After Louis II took Bari from the Arabs in 871, the Byzantines occupied it in 876 and, through the campaigns of Nikephoros Phokas the Elder in 885–886, recovered much of Apulia and Calabria. Around 891 these lands were organised as the Theme of Longobardia, named after its largely Lombard population.
theme-of-longobardia.r: A strategos governed from Bari, at times claiming overlordship over the Lombard principalities of Benevento, Capua and Salerno. The population was mostly Latin-speaking and lived under Lombard law, while Greek officials, settlers and monasteries brought Byzantine influence. Tax registers, charters and the building of fortified towns show an active administration.
theme-of-longobardia.e: Around 965–970 Longobardia was combined with Calabria and Lucania under a new, higher-ranking governor, the catepan, creating the Catepanate of Italy, which continued until the Norman conquest.

the-protectorate.t: The phase of the English republic in which Oliver Cromwell, and briefly his son Richard, ruled as Lord Protector of England, Scotland and Ireland.
the-protectorate.o: In December 1653, after the failure of Barebone's Parliament, army officers drew up the Instrument of Government, Britain's first written constitution, which made Oliver Cromwell Lord Protector of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland, with a Council of State and Parliament.
the-protectorate.r: Cromwell governed with mixed success: he quarrelled with his Parliaments, divided the country under the Major-Generals in 1655 to 1657 and refused the crown in 1657, accepting instead the Humble Petition and Advice. Abroad, the Protectorate made peace with the Dutch, fought Spain and seized Jamaica in 1655. Jews were readmitted to England in 1656.
the-protectorate.e: Oliver died in September 1658 and was succeeded by his son Richard, who lacked army support and resigned in May 1659. The Commonwealth of England was restored briefly before the Restoration of 1660.

tegea.t: Leading city of south-eastern Arcadia, long Sparta's rival and ally, famed for the temple of Athena Alea rebuilt by the sculptor Scopas.
tegea.o: Tegea formed from the union of nine villages in the high plain of south-eastern Arcadia, bordering Laconia. Its sanctuary of Athena Alea was a regional cult centre by the 8th century BCE. In the 6th century BCE Tegea defeated a Spartan invasion in the 'Battle of the Fetters', in which captured Spartans had to work Tegean fields in their own chains.
tegea.r: Sparta later prevailed, reportedly after recovering the bones of Orestes from Tegea, and Tegea became a leading member of the Peloponnesian League, fighting at Plataea in 479 BCE. Its temple of Athena Alea, burned in 395 BCE, was rebuilt by Scopas and was one of the finest in the Peloponnese.
tegea.e: After Leuctra, Tegea joined Mantinea in founding the Arcadian League in 370 BCE. In the Hellenistic period it passed among the Aetolian League, Sparta under Cleomenes III and the Achaean League, coming under Rome in 146 BCE.
tegea.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Alea

triboci.t: Germanic people who crossed the Rhine with Ariovistus and settled in northern Alsace around Brumath.
triboci.o: The Triboci appear in Caesar's account of the battle against Ariovistus in 58 BCE as one of the peoples in his army. They had settled on the left bank of the Rhine, in land previously held by the Mediomatrici.
triboci.r: Nothing is known of their institutions. They seem to have adopted Gallic ways quickly after settling west of the Rhine.
triboci.e: After Caesar's victory over Ariovistus they remained in Alsace. Under Rome they formed a civitas with its chief town at Brocomagus (Brumath), north of Strasbourg.

tyras.t: A Greek colony at the mouth of the Dniester whose site, later the fortress of Akkerman, was inhabited for more than two thousand years.
tyras.o: Settlers from Miletus founded Tyras around 600 BCE on the right bank of the Dniester estuary, at modern Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi. The town took its name from the river, which the Greeks called Tyras, and is sometimes linked with an earlier settlement called Ophiusa.
tyras.r: Tyras was a small self-governing polis run by magistrates and a council on the usual Greek model. It lived by trading wine, olive oil and fine pottery to the peoples of the hinterland in return for grain, fish, hides and slaves, and it minted its own coins. Its neighbours were in turn Scythians, Getae and Sarmatians.
tyras.e: The Getae of Burebista sacked the town around 50 BCE. It recovered under Roman protection from the 1st century CE, with a Roman garrison and links to the province of Moesia Inferior. Gothic raids in the 3rd century and the arrival of the Huns ended the ancient city, though the site was later rebuilt as Moncastro and Akkerman.

timocani.t: Slavic tribe of the Timok valley that broke from Bulgaria in 818 and sought the protection of the Frankish emperor.
timocani.o: The Timočani lived along the Timok river in modern eastern Serbia and north-western Bulgaria, among the Slavs who settled the area in the 7th century. They are known almost entirely from the Royal Frankish Annals.
timocani.r: Little is known of their society. In 818 their envoys came to Louis the Pious, having left the alliance of the Bulgarians, and they then joined the rising of Ljudevit of the Duchy of Pannonian Croatia against the Franks.
timocani.e: After 819 they disappear from the sources. The First Bulgarian Empire under Omurtag reasserted control over the middle Danube in the 820s, and the Timok valley remained Bulgarian.

teke.t: A Turkish beylik on the Mediterranean coast around Antalya, a branch of the Hamidids that briefly lost its capital to the King of Cyprus.
teke.o: In the early 14th century a branch of the Hamidids took control of Antalya and the surrounding coastland, known from its Turkmen inhabitants as Teke. Around 1321 it became a separate beylik.
teke.r: The beylik lived from Antalya's port, which traded with Cyprus, Egypt and the Italian republics. Ibn Battuta visited in the 1330s and met its ruler Khidr Bey. In 1361 Peter I of Cyprus captured Antalya, holding it until 1373, when the beylik regained it. The Teke rulers built mosques and a madrasa in Antalya.
teke.e: Bayezid I annexed Teke around 1390, and Timur restored it in 1402. Osman Bey, the last ruler, was killed besieging Antalya in 1423, and the Ottomans annexed the beylik.
