taifa-of-calatayud.t: A short-lived Hudid principality at Calatayud, created when the founder of the Hudid dynasty divided his lands among his sons.
taifa-of-calatayud.o: When Sulayman ibn Hud al-Mustain of the Taifa of Zaragoza died in 1046, his realm was split among his sons. Muhammad received Calatayud, an old town on the Jalón controlling the road from Zaragoza to Toledo.
taifa-of-calatayud.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, the principality was a fortified district rather than a full kingdom, and its ruler was quickly drawn into conflict with his ambitious brother Ahmad al-Muqtadir.
taifa-of-calatayud.e: By around 1055 al-Muqtadir had removed his brothers and reunited Calatayud with the Taifa of Zaragoza. Alfonso I of Aragon took the town in 1120.

taifa-of-seville.t: The most powerful taifa of al-Andalus, ruled by the Abbadids, whose poet-king al-Mutamid invited the Almoravids and lost his throne to them.
taifa-of-seville.o: In 1023 the leading families of Seville expelled the Hammudid garrison and entrusted the city to the qadi Abu al-Qasim Muhammad ibn Abbad, of an old Arab family. He ruled in the name of a shadowy pretender, supposedly the vanished caliph Hisham II, which gave the Abbadids a claim to wider authority.
taifa-of-seville.r: Al-Mutadid (1042-1069) expanded ruthlessly, annexing the Berber and Arab taifas of the south-west, from the Algarve to Ronda. His son al-Mutamid (1069-1091), himself a celebrated poet, added Córdoba in 1070 and Murcia in 1078, with the poet Ibn Ammar as vizier. Seville's olive oil, textiles and river port made it the wealthiest city in the west, though it paid tribute to Castile.
taifa-of-seville.e: After Toledo fell in 1085, al-Mutamid called in the Almoravids, who won at Sagrajas in 1086 but deposed him in 1091. He died in exile at Aghmat in Morocco, and his poems of loss became classics of Arabic literature.

terek-cossack-host.t: The self-governing Cossack community of the Terek river, for over three centuries Russia's armed frontier society in the North Caucasus.
terek-cossack-host.o: Free Cossacks from the Don and Volga settled on the lower Terek in the 16th century, and the Greben Cossacks lived in the foothills. The host traditionally dates its founding to 1577, when Russian Cossacks were recorded on the Terek after Muscovy's push down the Volga to Astrakhan. They served the Tsardom of Russia in return for pay and freedoms.
terek-cossack-host.r: Cossack villages, or stanitsas, elected atamans and held assemblies, combining farming, fishing, vineyards and horse breeding with military service. Many were Old Believers. Under the Russian Empire the host manned the fortified Caucasian Line from Kizlyar and Mozdok, was steadily placed under state control, and was formally reorganised in 1860 with its centre at Vladikavkaz.
terek-cossack-host.e: After 1917 the Terek Cossacks briefly joined the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus, then fought the Bolsheviks. In 1920 the Russian SFSR crushed them, abolished the host and deported many stanitsas, giving their lands to Chechens and Ingush.

theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes.t: Upper Egypt ruled by the High Priests of Amun at Thebes, who governed through the god's oracle at the end of the New Kingdom.
theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes.o: As the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom disintegrated under Ramesses XI, the general and High Priest of Amun Herihor took control of Thebes around 1080 BCE and even wrote his name in a royal cartouche. The country was divided: the Twenty-first Dynasty of Egypt ruled the north from Tanis while the high priests held the south.
theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes.r: The high priests were also army commanders, and they ruled from Thebes in the name of Amun, whose oracle was consulted on appointments, property and justice. They nominally recognised the Tanite kings, and the two houses intermarried. Pinedjem I took royal titles. Faced with tomb robbery, the priests moved the royal mummies to caches such as Deir el-Bahari tomb DB320, where many were found in 1881.
theocracy-of-amun-at-thebes.e: Around 943 BCE Sheshonq I of the Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt installed his own son Iuput as High Priest, ending the independent theocracy. The office kept great prestige, and power at Thebes later passed to the God's Wife of Amun.

taifa-of-lisbon.t: A brief taifa at Lisbon on the Tagus estuary, held by the heirs of the freedman Sabur before its absorption by Badajoz.
taifa-of-lisbon.o: Lisbon had been part of the territory controlled by the freedman Sabur al-Saqlabi from Badajoz. When he died in 1022 and his vizier seized Badajoz, Sabur's sons are said to have kept Lisbon as a separate principality.
taifa-of-lisbon.r: Known only from a few lines in Arabic chronicles, the taifa consisted of Lisbon and its estuary, an Atlantic port trading in fish, salt and agricultural produce. Its rulers had no lasting dynasty or court to speak of.
taifa-of-lisbon.e: By 1034 the Aftasids of the Taifa of Badajoz had absorbed Lisbon. It stayed under Badajoz until 1093, then passed to the Almoravids, and Afonso I of the Kingdom of Portugal took it in 1147 with the help of crusaders.

tusculum.t: Latin hill town in the Alban Hills, once a leader of the Latins against Rome, which in 381 BCE became the first community given Roman citizenship.
tusculum.o: Tusculum stood on a high ridge of the Alban Hills above modern Frascati, overlooking the routes south-east from Rome. Legend made Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe, its founder. It was an important Latin town by the 6th century BCE, with links to Rome's last kings.
tusculum.r: Its leading family, the Mamilii, intermarried with the Tarquins; Octavius Mamilius, son-in-law of Tarquinius Superbus, is said to have led the Latins against Rome at Lake Regillus around 496 BCE. Afterwards Tusculum became one of Rome's most loyal allies in the wars against the Aequi and Volsci, and it hosted shrines of Castor and Pollux, gods also linked to Regillus.
tusculum.e: In 381 BCE, after a brief suspicion of disloyalty, Rome granted Tusculum full citizenship while letting it keep its own magistrates, making it the first municipium. It produced leading Roman families, among them that of Cato the Elder, and Cicero's villa there gave its name to his Tusculan Disputations.

taceddinids.t: A small Turkmen beylik around Niksar in the hinterland of the Black Sea, closely tied by marriage to the Empire of Trebizond.
taceddinids.o: As Eretnid authority weakened in the mid 14th century, local Turkmen chiefs took control of the Pontic hinterland between Niksar and the coast. One of them, Taceddin Bey, founded a beylik around Niksar.
taceddinids.r: The beylik held the inland valleys and parts of the coast near Unye and ruled Turkmen tribes, including the Chepni. Its relations with the Empire of Trebizond mixed raiding and alliance: Taceddin married a daughter of Alexios III. Taceddin died fighting Trebizond in 1362. The beylik was later drawn into the struggles between Kadi Burhan al-Din and the Ottomans.
taceddinids.e: The beylik came under Ottoman control in the early 15th century and was absorbed around 1428.

tajik-assr.t: The first Tajik national republic, created in 1924 as an autonomous part of Soviet Uzbekistan.
tajik-assr.o: In the national delimitation of 1924 the mainly Tajik-speaking mountain districts of eastern Bukhara and the Pamirs were organised as the Tajik ASSR within the Uzbek SSR. The village of Dushanbe was chosen as capital and grew rapidly.
tajik-assr.r: The republic was a poor, mountainous territory still fighting the last Basmachi bands. Soviet authorities built roads, schools and irrigation for cotton, and promoted the Tajik language, which was written in a Latin alphabet from 1928. Tajik intellectuals argued that Samarkand and Bukhara, both Tajik-speaking cities, had been wrongly given to Uzbekistan.
tajik-assr.e: In 1929 the republic was separated from Uzbekistan and raised to a union republic, the Tajik SSR, with the Khujand region added. Dushanbe was renamed Stalinabad.

tanagra.t: Boeotian city famed for its painted terracotta figurines and the poet Corinna, and site of the battle where Sparta defeated Athens in 457 BCE.
tanagra.o: Tanagra lay in eastern Boeotia on a hill above the Asopus valley, near the border with Attica. Settled since the Bronze Age, it was a city by the Archaic period and a member of the Boeotian League, often second only to Thebes.
tanagra.r: Tanagra was the home of the lyric poet Corinna, said to have competed with Pindar. In 457 BCE Sparta and its allies defeated Athens at the Battle of Tanagra, though Athens won at nearby Oenophyta soon afterwards and controlled Boeotia for a decade. In the 4th century BCE Tanagra's workshops produced elegant terracotta figurines of women, now called Tanagras.
tanagra.e: Tanagra survived Theban dominance and the Macedonian period as a prosperous town and came under Roman control in 146 BCE. Its cemeteries, looted in the 1870s, filled museums with its figurines.

tuttul.t: Tuttul, a city on the Euphrates near modern Raqqa, sacred to the god Dagan, where Sargon of Akkad prayed before conquering the upper Euphrates.
tuttul.o: Tuttul stood at Tell Bi'a where the Balikh river meets the Euphrates, an ideal place for river and caravan traffic. It was a substantial city by the mid-3rd millennium BCE and became famous as the cult centre of Dagan, the chief god of the middle Euphrates.
tuttul.r: Sargon of the Akkadian Empire recorded that he bowed to Dagan at Tuttul, who granted him Mari, Ebla and the cedar forests. In the 18th century BCE Tuttul was a seat of Amorite tribal kings who fought Yahdun-Lim of Mari, and later fell under Shamshi-Adad and Zimri-Lim. German excavations from 1980 uncovered palaces and tombs.
tuttul.e: After Hammurabi of the Babylonian Empire destroyed Mari, Tuttul declined and lost its independence around 1760 BCE. It remained a minor settlement, and its sanctuary of Dagan faded from the record.

taifa-of-granada.t: The Zirid kingdom of Granada, founded by Sanhaja Berbers, which made Granada a major city and left a rare royal memoir by its last king.
taifa-of-granada.o: Around 1013 the Sanhaja Berber leader Zawi ibn Ziri, a veteran of the caliphal wars, took over the district of Elvira and moved its centre to the more defensible hill of Granada. His nephew Habbus established the dynasty when Zawi returned to Ifriqiya.
taifa-of-granada.r: Badis (1038-1073) built much of the Alcazaba and ruled with the Jewish vizier Samuel ibn Naghrela, a poet and general, and then his son Joseph. Resentment against Joseph led to the Granada massacre of 1066. The kingdom fought Almería and Seville and paid heavy tribute to Castile.
taifa-of-granada.e: The Almoravids deposed the last king, Abd Allah ibn Buluggin, in 1090 and exiled him to Aghmat, where he wrote his memoirs, a unique first-hand account of taifa politics. Granada later became the capital of the Emirate of Granada.

turduli.t: A people of the south-west, close kin of the Turdetani, with a northern branch, the Turduli Veteres, living near the Douro in Portugal.
turduli.o: The Turduli lived in the middle Guadiana and Guadalquivir regions next to the Turdetani, from whom Strabo said they could hardly be distinguished. A separate group, the Turduli Veteres or Old Turduli, settled south of the lower Douro in northern Portugal, probably after migrating from the south.
turduli.r: Little is recorded of their government. Their economy relied on farming, herding and the mineral wealth of the Sierra Morena. Pliny lists their towns in both Baetica and Lusitania, which shows how widespread the group was.
turduli.e: They were absorbed into Roman Hispania Ulterior during the 2nd century BCE, following the conquest of the south after 206 BCE and the Lusitanian wars. Under Augustus their lands were divided between Baetica and Lusitania.

taranchi-sultanate.t: A short-lived Muslim sultanate in the Ili valley that rose during the Dungan revolt and was occupied by Russia in 1871.
taranchi-sultanate.o: In 1864 a rebellion of Hui (Dungan) and Turkic Muslims against Qing rule spread across Xinjiang. In the Ili valley, the Taranchis, Uyghur farmers descended from settlers brought by the Dzungars, joined the Dungans, captured the Qing garrisons of Ili, including Huiyuan, and established a sultanate at Ghulja.
taranchi-sultanate.r: The Taranchi leader Abil Oghlu became sultan in 1866 after the Taranchis turned on the Dungans. The sultanate ruled a farming population in the Ili valley, under Islamic law, and dealt with Russian merchants and neighbouring Yettishar.
taranchi-sultanate.e: Fearing that Yaqub Beg of Yettishar would take Ili and alarmed by instability on its frontier, Russia occupied the Ili valley in 1871, ending the sultanate. Russia returned most of the region to the Qing under the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881.

transvaal-colony.t: The British colony made from the conquered Transvaal republic, rebuilt around the gold mines of the Witwatersrand.
transvaal-colony.o: British forces occupied Pretoria in June 1900 and Britain proclaimed the annexation of the South African Republic in September 1900. The Treaty of Vereeniging in May 1902 ended Boer resistance and confirmed the Transvaal Colony.
transvaal-colony.r: High Commissioner Lord Milner's administration rebuilt railways and farms and restarted the gold mines, recruiting young British administrators known as Milner's Kindergarten. To solve a labour shortage, more than 60,000 Chinese indentured labourers were brought to the mines between 1904 and 1907, a scandal in Britain. Self-government came in 1907, and the Het Volk party of Louis Botha and Jan Smuts won the election.
transvaal-colony.e: Botha and Smuts led the negotiations for union, and in 1910 the Transvaal joined the Union of South Africa as the Transvaal Province, with Pretoria as the administrative capital of the new state.

taqali.t: A Muslim kingdom in the Nuba Mountains of Kordofan whose kings, the meks, kept their throne for over four centuries until 1969.
taqali.o: Taqali arose in the hills of the north-eastern Nuba Mountains in the early 16th century. Its traditions tell of a Muslim holy man from the Nile who married into a local ruling family, founding a dynasty that drew on both Islamic and Nuba roots, with its seat at Tasi.
taqali.r: The meks ruled a mixed population of Nuba hill farmers and Arab settlers, protected by rugged terrain. Taqali paid tribute at times to the Funj Sultanate and fought off raids from the Musabba'at sultanate and the Darfur Sultanate. It traded slaves, gold and cattle with the Nile valley and served as a centre of Islam in the Nuba Mountains.
taqali.e: Taqali survived Turco-Egyptian Sudan as a tributary; Mek Adam Umm Dabbalo supported the Mahdist State. Under Anglo-Egyptian Sudan the meks served as native administrators. Sudan's government abolished the native administration system in 1969, ending the kingdom's official role.

tencteri.t: A Germanic people of the lower Rhine famous for their cavalry, nearly destroyed by Caesar in 55 BCE yet still present in Roman sources centuries later.
tencteri.o: The Tencteri and their neighbours the Usipetes were driven from their homes by the Suebi and crossed the Rhine into Gaul in 55 BCE. Julius Caesar attacked them during negotiations near the Meuse and Rhine and massacred large numbers, an act condemned at the time in the Roman Senate. The survivors fled to the Sugambri.
tencteri.r: Tacitus singles out the Tencteri for their horsemanship, writing that the horses and herds passed to the bravest son rather than simply to the eldest. They lived on the right bank of the Rhine opposite Cologne and dealt with the Roman city of the Ubii. In 16 BCE they joined the Sugambri in defeating Marcus Lollius.
tencteri.e: The Tencteri appear in the Batavian revolt of 69 and are last mentioned in the late Roman period. By the later 3rd century their territory lay within the area of the Frankish confederation, into which they were most likely absorbed.

tyre.t: Tyre, the island city that led Phoenician trade across the Mediterranean, founded Carthage and resisted Alexander in a seven-month siege.
tyre.o: Tyre was built on an offshore island with a mainland suburb, giving it a nearly impregnable harbour. It was a vassal of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom in the Amarna age under King Abimilki, and after the Late Bronze Age collapse it emerged in the 10th century BCE as the strongest Phoenician city.
tyre.r: Its kings, such as Hiram I, ally of Solomon of the United Kingdom of Israel, ruled a merchant state with the temple of Melqart at its heart. Tyre produced murex purple dye and glass, and its sailors founded colonies across the western Mediterranean, including Carthage, traditionally in 814 BCE.
tyre.e: Tyre paid tribute to the Assyrian Empire and survived a 13-year siege by Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire. Under the Achaemenid Empire it kept its kings. In 332 BCE Alexander of the Macedonian Empire built a causeway, stormed the island and sold its people into slavery.

thamud.t: An ancient Arab people of the Hejaz, known from Assyrian annals to the Quran, whose name lives on in thousands of rock inscriptions.
thamud.o: The Thamud are first named among Arab groups defeated by Sargon II of the Assyrian Empire in 715 BCE. They lived in north-western Arabia, between the Hejaz and the Nafud, and later Greek and Roman writers such as Diodorus, Pliny and Ptolemy also place them there.
thamud.r: They seem to have been a confederation of herding and oasis tribes rather than a centralised kingdom. Their name was given by modern scholars to a large body of Ancient North Arabian graffiti, though not all were written by Thamud. At Ruwafa, Thamudic tribesmen built a temple in the 160s CE honouring the Roman emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.
thamud.e: Around 400 CE Roman lists record a cavalry unit of Thamudeni in Egypt and Palestine, after which they disappear. The Quran tells of the Thamud as a people destroyed for rejecting the prophet Salih, and links them to the rock tombs of Hegra, which were in fact Nabataean.

tippu-tips-state.t: The commercial empire of the Zanzibari trader Tippu Tip on the upper Congo, built on ivory and slaves and broken by the Congo Free State.
tippu-tips-state.o: Hamed bin Muhammad al-Murjebi, called Tippu Tip, was a Swahili-Arab trader from Zanzibar who led caravans deep into the interior from the 1860s. Around 1870 he established himself in Manyema on the upper Lualaba, making Kasongo the centre of a domain of trading posts, allied chiefs and armed followers.
tippu-tips-state.r: The state was a commercial network rather than a kingdom: armed bands collected ivory and captives, plantations of rice and other crops fed the settlements, and goods moved east to Zanzibar. Tippu Tip helped Henry Morton Stanley down the Lualaba in 1876, and in 1887 the Congo Free State appointed him governor of the Stanley Falls district.
tippu-tips-state.e: Tippu Tip retired to Zanzibar in 1890. War broke out between the Free State and the Swahili-Arab traders in 1892, Kasongo fell in 1893, and by 1894 the state had been destroyed, its lands absorbed into the Congo Free State.

tyumen-khanate.t: A Shibanid khanate of western Siberia that briefly ruled the Golden Horde's eastern steppes and was the forerunner of the Khanate of Sibir.
tyumen-khanate.o: The Tyumen Khanate grew from the old Ulus of Shiban around Chimgi-Tura on the Tura River in the early 15th century, as Golden Horde authority faded. Shibanid princes ruled there, and the khan Abu'l-Khayr was proclaimed in this region in 1428 before moving south.
tyumen-khanate.r: The khanate ruled Tatar nomads and the forest peoples of western Siberia, collecting tribute in furs that were traded south and west. Its most notable ruler, Ibak Khan, took part in the destruction of the Great Horde, killing its khan Ahmad in 1481 after the Great Stand on the Ugra River, and claimed leadership among the Jochids.
tyumen-khanate.e: Around 1495 the local Taibugid clan seized power, killing Ibak and moving the capital to Qashliq on the Irtysh, founding the Khanate of Sibir. Chimgi-Tura was later rebuilt by the Russians as Tyumen in 1586.

tetrarchy-of-philip.t: The north-eastern share of Herod the Great's kingdom, ruled for almost four decades by his son Philip from the new city of Caesarea Philippi.
tetrarchy-of-philip.o: When Herod the Great died in 4 BCE, Augustus confirmed his will with changes and divided the kingdom among three sons. Philip received the lands north and east of the Sea of Galilee: Gaulanitis, Batanaea, Trachonitis, Auranitis and part of Ituraea, a frontier zone the Romans had entrusted to Herod to suppress brigandage.
tetrarchy-of-philip.r: Philip governed as a Roman client with the title tetrarch. His subjects were largely Syrian, Arab and Greek-speaking pagans with Jewish communities, and he was the first Jewish ruler to put the emperor's portrait on his coins. He refounded Paneas at the springs of the Jordan as Caesarea Philippi and raised Bethsaida to a city named Julias. Josephus describes him as a mild, accessible ruler who travelled his territory to judge cases.
tetrarchy-of-philip.e: Philip died in 34 CE without children, and Tiberius attached the tetrarchy to the province of Syria. In 37 Caligula granted it to Herod Agrippa I, making it the core of the Kingdom of Herod Agrippa. Caesarea Philippi remains known from the Gospels as the place of Peter's confession.

turdetani.t: The heirs of Tartessos in the lower Guadalquivir, praised by Strabo as the most cultured of the Iberians, with written laws in verse.
turdetani.o: The Turdetani appear after the decline of Tartessos around 500 BCE, occupying the same rich lower Guadalquivir valley in modern Seville, Huelva and Cádiz. Ancient writers saw them as the successors of the Tartessians.
turdetani.r: They lived in many towns ruled by local kings and aristocracies. Strabo called them the wisest of the Iberians, said to have laws in verse and an ancient literature. Their land produced grain, olive oil and wine and held the silver and copper of the Sierra Morena and Río Tinto. They were heavily influenced by Gadir and the other Phoenician cities, and later by Carthage.
turdetani.e: Under Barcid Iberia they supplied silver and troops. After 206 BCE Rome took control; Culchas, who ruled 28 towns, first aided Rome and then joined the revolt of 197 BCE. Defeated, they became the core of Hispania Ulterior and later Baetica.

turk-shahis.t: A Turkic dynasty that ruled Kabul and Gandhara for over 150 years, blocking the Arab advance into the Indian subcontinent.
turk-shahis.o: Around 665 a Turkic dynasty, probably linked to the Western Turkic Khaganate and Tokharistan, replaced the Nezak Huns in Kabul and Kapisa. Its founder Barha Tegin claimed a long descent, and al-Biruni later recorded traditions of a line of sixty kings.
turk-shahis.r: The Turk Shahis ruled a largely Buddhist and Hindu population from Kabul, and later also Gandhara, issuing coins with Bactrian and Brahmi legends. They received Tang Chinese titles; Tegin Shah was recognised in the 720s. Allied with the Zunbils to the south, they repeatedly fought off Arab armies from Sistan and Khurasan.
turk-shahis.e: In the early 9th century the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun forced the last Turk Shahi king to submit and convert, and soon after, around 822, the Brahmin minister Kallar overthrew the dynasty, founding the Hindu Shahis.

taifa-of-murcia.t: A south-eastern taifa that shifted between local rulers and powerful neighbours before falling to the Almoravids, with Murcia's huerta as its core.
taifa-of-murcia.o: Murcia, heir to the old Visigothic-era region of Tudmir, broke from Córdoba around 1011. For its first decades it was usually governed for the Amirid rulers of Almería and Valencia, until the local family of the Banu Tahir took effective control under Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn Tahir.
taifa-of-murcia.r: The Segura valley's irrigation supported grain, fruit and textile production. The Banu Tahir ruled as patricians, nominally under Valencia. In 1078 al-Mutamid of the Taifa of Seville sent his vizier, the poet Ibn Ammar, to seize the city; Ibn Ammar and then his officer Ibn Rashiq ruled it in defiance of Seville.
taifa-of-murcia.e: Ibn Rashiq's double dealing with Castile, which held the nearby fortress of Aledo, made him unpopular. The Almoravids took Murcia in 1091. It re-emerged as the Second Taifa of Murcia in 1147.

taifa-of-guadix.t: A short-lived highland taifa around Guadix and Baza, east of Granada, formed during the revolts against the Almoravids.
taifa-of-guadix.o: In 1145, as the Almoravid regime in al-Andalus disintegrated, local leaders took control of Guadix and Baza, two towns on the high plateau between Granada and the coast at Almería region.
taifa-of-guadix.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, the state was centred on irrigated basins and cave settlements and controlled the route from Granada to the east coast. Its leaders were caught between Ibn Mardanish of Murcia, the Almoravid loyalists of Granada and the Almohads.
taifa-of-guadix.e: Around 1151 the district passed under Almohad control. Guadix later belonged to the Emirate of Granada until 1489.

tatar-confederation.t: A powerful group of tribes in eastern Mongolia, enemies of Genghis Khan's family, whose name Europeans later applied to all the Mongol peoples.
tatar-confederation.o: Tatars appear in Old Turkic inscriptions of the 8th century as the Otuz Tatar and Toquz Tatar. By the 10th century tribes under this name occupied the grasslands of eastern Mongolia around Lakes Hulun and Buir, a numerous and wealthy people organised in several clans under their own chiefs.
tatar-confederation.r: They lived by pastoral nomadism, herding horses, cattle and sheep, and traded and fought with their settled neighbours. The Jin dynasty (1115-1234) used them as allies against other steppe peoples; according to the Secret History of the Mongols they handed the Mongol leader Ambaghai to the Jin for execution and poisoned Temüjin's father Yesügei. There was no lasting central government.
tatar-confederation.e: In 1196 the Jin, with Temüjin and the Keraite ruler Toghrul, defeated the Tatar chief Megüjin Seultü. In 1202 Temüjin crushed the remaining Tatars and had most of their men killed, absorbing the survivors into the future Mongol Empire.

taifa-of-zaragoza.t: The powerful taifa of the Ebro valley whose Hudid kings built the Aljafería palace, employed El Cid and held off Christian advance until 1110.
taifa-of-zaragoza.o: Zaragoza, capital of the Upper March, came under the Arab Tujibid governor Mundhir I around 1018. In 1039 the Tujibids were overthrown and Sulayman ibn Hud al-Mustain founded the Hudid dynasty, which went on to rule for some seventy years.
taifa-of-zaragoza.r: Ahmad I al-Muqtadir (1046-1081) annexed Tortosa and Dénia and built the Aljafería palace. His son Yusuf al-Mutaman wrote a major treatise on geometry. The kingdom paid tribute to Castile and Barcelona and from 1081 employed El Cid against Aragon. Its farmland, trade and learning made it one of the richest taifas.
taifa-of-zaragoza.e: Ahmad II al-Mustain was killed fighting Aragon at Valtierra in 1110, and the Almoravids then took Zaragoza. His son held on at Rueda de Jalón (Hudid). Alfonso I of Aragon captured Zaragoza in 1118.

tapajo.t: A large chiefdom at the meeting of the Tapajós and Amazon rivers, known for its intricate pottery and dark earth soils.
tapajo.o: The Tapajó people dominated the lower Tapajós river around the site of modern Santarém in Brazil from about 1000. The Santarém culture associated with them developed from earlier Amazonian traditions, and its main settlement covered several square kilometres.
tapajo.r: Spanish and Portuguese explorers in the 16th and 17th centuries described a numerous people under powerful chiefs who could field many warriors armed with poisoned arrows. The Tapajó farmed on terra preta, fertile dark earth created by long settlement, and fished in the rivers. Their potters made elaborate caryatid vessels and vases decorated with modelled animals and figures, and they carved green stone pendants called muiraquitãs.
tapajo.e: Portuguese slaving expeditions from the 1620s and the founding of a Jesuit mission in 1661, which became Santarém, ended Tapajó independence. Epidemics and enslavement destroyed most of the population. The Santarém ceramic style is today among the best known Amazonian archaeological traditions.

taifa-of-alpuente.t: One of the smallest taifas of al-Andalus, a Berber-ruled mountain lordship in the hills north-west of Valencia that outlasted many larger rivals.
taifa-of-alpuente.o: Around 1009, as caliphal authority collapsed, the Banu Qasim, a family of Berber origin settled in the Valencian uplands, made the fortress town of Alpuente the centre of their own principality under Abd Allah ibn Qasim, who took the honorific Yumn al-Dawla.
taifa-of-alpuente.r: The state covered little more than a cluster of castles and valleys in the Serranía, living from herding, dry farming and control of routes between Valencia and Aragon. Its survival depended on its remoteness and on careful diplomacy with Toledo, Valencia and Zaragoza. Few details of its internal life are recorded.
taifa-of-alpuente.e: The Almoravids, who unified al-Andalus after 1090, absorbed Alpuente around 1106. The town later passed under Almohad rule and was taken by the Crown of Aragon in the 13th century.

taras.t: The only Spartan colony in Italy, which grew into the leading Greek city of southern Italy and fought Rome with the help of Pyrrhus.
taras.o: Tradition says that the Partheniai, sons of Spartan women born during the Messenian War, were sent out under Phalanthus and founded Taras in 706 BCE. The city occupied a peninsula between the Mar Piccolo lagoon and the open sea, giving it the best harbour on the Gulf of Taranto.
taras.r: Taras grew rich on fishing, purple dye, fine wool, horses and pottery; Apulian red-figure vases were made there. After a heavy defeat by the Iapygians around 473 BCE it became a democracy. In the 4th century BCE the philosopher Archytas, a friend of Plato, was repeatedly elected general. Taras led the Italiote League and hired Greek commanders, including Archidamus III of Sparta and Alexander of Epirus, against Italic peoples.
taras.e: Conflict with Rome began in 282 BCE when Tarentines attacked a Roman squadron. Pyrrhus of Epirus came to their aid, but after his departure Taras surrendered in 272 BCE. It defected to Hannibal in 212 BCE and was sacked when retaken in 209 BCE. Roman Tarentum survives as Taranto.

tanukhids.t: An Arab tribal confederation that served Rome as allied frontier troops in Syria, remembered for Queen Mavia's revolt against the emperor Valens.
tanukhids.o: Arabic tradition says the Tanukh were a coalition of tribes that migrated from eastern Arabia into Iraq, where some settled around al-Hira, while others moved into Syria in the later 3rd century. There they became foederati, allies who guarded the desert frontier for Rome in return for subsidies.
tanukhids.r: The Tanukhids were pastoral and semi-settled Arabs who adopted Christianity during the 4th century. Their best-known leader is Mavia, who around 378 led a revolt that ravaged Palestine and Phoenicia and ended only when Valens agreed to her demand for an orthodox Arab hermit, Moses, as bishop of her people. Her troops then helped defend Constantinople against the Goths after the battle of Adrianople. Little else about their organisation is recorded.
tanukhids.e: In the 5th century the Salihids replaced them as Rome's leading Arab allies. Tanukh clans remained in northern Syria around Qinnasrin and Aleppo, accepted Islam after the Arab conquest, and later Tanukhid families played a part in the history of Mount Lebanon.

twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The Saite Dynasty, which freed Egypt from Assyrian and Kushite control and gave it a last long era of native prosperity.
twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Psamtik I, son of the Saite ruler Necho I, began in 664 BCE as an Assyrian vassal after Assyria drove out the Kushite Empire. As Assyria weakened he threw off its overlordship, and in 656 BCE he took Thebes peacefully by having his daughter Nitocris adopted as the future God's Wife of Amun.
twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Saite kings relied on Greek and Carian mercenaries and allowed Greek traders to settle at Naukratis. Necho II began a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea, sent a Phoenician fleet around Africa and killed King Josiah of Judah at Megiddo, but lost to Babylon at Carchemish in 605 BCE. Art and texts deliberately revived Old Kingdom models, and the Demotic script came into use. Amasis II courted Greek cities.
twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: In 525 BCE the Persian king Cambyses II defeated Psamtik III at Pelusium and took Memphis, turning the country into Achaemenid Egypt. Saite art and religion shaped Late Period Egypt, and Greek knowledge of Egypt, through Herodotus, rests largely on this era.

troezen.t: Small city of the eastern Argolid, mythical birthplace of Theseus, which sheltered Athenian families during Xerxes's invasion of 480 BCE.
troezen.o: Troezen lay on the Argolid peninsula facing the Saronic Gulf, with Ionian traditions shared with Athens and later Dorian settlement. Myth made it the birthplace of Theseus and the home of his grandfather Pittheus. In the Archaic period it was a small independent city with a harbour at Pogon.
troezen.r: Troezenians helped found Halicarnassus and, with Achaeans, Sybaris in Italy. In 480 BCE Athenian women and children were evacuated to Troezen before Salamis, as recorded in the inscribed Troezen Decree found in 1959. Troezen fought at Salamis and Plataea and was usually a member of the Peloponnesian League. It had a sanctuary of Hippolytus.
troezen.e: In the Hellenistic period Troezen changed hands among Macedonian kings and Sparta before joining the Achaean League. It passed under Roman control in 146 BCE and continued as a small town.
troezen.re: Greek religion; cults of Hippolytus and Poseidon

tetouan-under-al-mandri.t: Tetouan refounded by exiles from Granada under the al-Mandri family, a corsair city ruled for a time by the famous Sayyida al-Hurra.
tetouan-under-al-mandri.o: Tetouan had lain in ruins since a Castilian raid around 1400. Around 1484, Ali al-Mandri, a military leader from the Emirate of Granada, rebuilt the town with Andalusi refugees, with permission from the Wattasid Sultanate, as a base against the Portuguese at Ceuta.
tetouan-under-al-mandri.r: The Andalusi elite ran Tetouan as an autonomous city, rebuilding walls and the medina in Granadan style. Corsairs operating from its river raided Spanish and Portuguese shipping and coasts, bringing captives for ransom. After al-Mandri's death his widow Sayyida al-Hurra, daughter of the founder of the Emirate of Chefchaouen, governed from about 1515 to 1542 and dealt directly with Portugal and Spain.
tetouan-under-al-mandri.e: Sayyida al-Hurra was deposed in 1542, and the Mandri family's influence waned as the Saadi Sultanate extended its control over northern Morocco in the 1560s. The Andalusi heritage of Tetouan's medina, now a UNESCO World Heritage site, remains.

territory-of-inini.t: The vast forested interior of French Guiana, governed as a separate territory from 1930 to 1946 in an attempt to develop it apart from the coast.
territory-of-inini.o: In 1930 France separated the interior of French Guiana from the coastal colony, creating the Territory of Inini. The aim was to develop the gold-rich forests and administer the indigenous and maroon peoples directly, outside the control of the coastal elected council.
territory-of-inini.r: Inini was governed directly by the governor of French Guiana, with its nominal capital at Saint-Élie, a gold-mining settlement. Gold prospecting was the main economic activity, and there was little infrastructure beyond river transport. The territory covered most of French Guiana's land but held only a small population of indigenous Amerindian peoples, maroon communities and gold miners.
territory-of-inini.e: In 1946, when French Guiana became an overseas department of France, Inini was merged back into it, though the interior kept a separate administrative status until 1969. Its former area now forms the interior communes of French Guiana, home to Amerindian and maroon communities.

twenty-fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The brief Saite kingdom of Tefnakht and Bakenranef, which challenged the Kushites for control of Egypt.
twenty-fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Tefnakht, Great Chief of the Libu and the Ma at Sais in the western Delta, united much of the Delta and Middle Egypt in the 720s BCE. His advance south provoked the invasion of Piye of the Kushite Empire around 728 BCE, after which Tefnakht submitted but kept his power and took royal titles.
twenty-fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: Its kings controlled the western Delta and Memphis and drew on the wealth of Delta trade with the Mediterranean. Bakenranef, called Bocchoris by the Greeks, was remembered in Greek tradition as a wise lawgiver who reformed contract law. A vase with his name found in an Etruscan tomb at Tarquinia shows Saite trade links.
twenty-fourth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 720 BCE the Kushite king Shabaka conquered the Delta; Manetho says he burned Bakenranef alive. The Saite family survived as local rulers and re-emerged as the Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt.

taifa-of-ceuta.t: A taifa across the Strait in Ceuta and Tangier, founded by a former Hammudid slave commander and the last obstacle to Almoravid control of the Strait.
taifa-of-ceuta.o: Ceuta had been a Hammudid possession. Around 1061 Suqut al-Barghawati, a commander of slave origin who had served the Hammudids, made himself independent there and in Tangier, ruling the African shore of the Strait of Gibraltar.
taifa-of-ceuta.r: Suqut controlled the vital ports linking al-Andalus to Morocco and maintained ties with the taifas, including the Taifa of Seville. His state was essentially a military regime defending the coast against the Almoravid Empire, which was expanding across Morocco.
taifa-of-ceuta.e: The Almoravids took Tangier in 1077, killing the aged Suqut in battle, and captured Ceuta from his son around 1083-1084. Control of Ceuta allowed them to cross into Iberia in 1086.

theban-eleventh-dynasty.t: The Theban kings who rose from local governors to reunite Egypt at the end of the First Intermediate Period.
theban-eleventh-dynasty.o: Around 2134 BCE the governors of the Theban nome, led by Mentuhotep I and Intef I, broke with the Herakleopolitan Kingdom and claimed royal titles. Thebes, until then a minor provincial town, became the capital of a southern kingdom stretching from Elephantine to the region of Abydos.
theban-eleventh-dynasty.r: Intef II, who reigned for about fifty years, fought the north for Thinis and Abydos and expanded the kingdom. The early kings were buried in large rock-cut 'saff' tombs at el-Tarif on the west bank of Thebes. They promoted the war god Montu and the local god Amun, and relied on Nubian archers, some of whom settled at Gebelein.
theban-eleventh-dynasty.e: Mentuhotep II defeated Herakleopolis and reunited the country around 2055 BCE, a date often used for the start of the Middle Kingdom of Egypt. His mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari set a model for later Theban royal building.

talava.t: Latgalian principality in north-eastern Latvia whose ruler Tālivaldis allied with the German crusaders against the Estonians.
talava.o: Tālava was a Latgalian territory in what is now north-eastern Latvia, with its main stronghold at Beverīna. It appears in Henry of Livonia's chronicle in the early 13th century, when it paid tribute to Pskov and was ruled by the elder Tālivaldis.
talava.r: Tālava's rulers led a Latgalian society of farmers and warriors with hillforts. Facing raids from the Estonians of Sakala and Ugandi, Tālivaldis and his sons Rameķis and Varibulis accepted Latin baptism around 1208 and joined the Germans and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in campaigns northwards.
talava.e: In 1215 raiders from Sakala captured Tālivaldis and roasted him to death. His sons kept a subordinate role, but in 1224 Tālava was divided between the bishop of Riga and the Sword Brothers. It became part of Terra Mariana, and the Latgalians merged into the Latvian people.

turpan-khanate.t: The eastern successor of the Chagatai Khanate, ruling Turpan and Hami, where Islam finally displaced the region's old Buddhist culture.
turpan-khanate.o: After Moghulistan divided in the 1460s, the eastern branch under Esen Buqa II's son Dost Muhammad and grandson Kebek Sultan controlled Turpan, which became its capital. The khanate is sometimes called Eastern Moghulistan or Uyghurstan.
turpan-khanate.r: The Turpan khans ruled the oases of Turpan, Kara-Shahr and at times Hami, controlling trade routes into China. Under Sultan Ahmad Khan and his son Mansur Khan they fought the Ming for Hami, and Islamisation of the Turpan Uyghurs was largely completed in this period, ending a long Buddhist tradition. The khanate was linked by marriage and rivalry to the Yarkent Khanate.
turpan-khanate.e: The Turpan khanate was weakened by divisions and absorbed into the Yarkent Khanate in the 17th century. In 1680 the Dzungar Khanate conquered both, bringing the oases under Oirat rule.

taulantii.t: Illyrian kingdom around Epidamnus on the Albanian coast, whose king Glaukias fought Alexander the Great and raised the young Pyrrhus.
taulantii.o: The Taulantii held the coastal plain around Epidamnus (Durrës) from at least the 5th century BCE; Thucydides records them in the quarrel over Epidamnus that helped spark the Peloponnesian War. By the 4th century BCE they were ruled by kings.
taulantii.r: Their kings controlled the hinterland of the Greek colonies of Epidamnus and Apollonia, trading with them and at times dominating them. In 335 BCE Glaukias joined Cleitus of Illyria against Alexander at Pelion. Glaukias later sheltered the infant Pyrrhus of Epirus and in 312 BCE seized Epidamnus.
taulantii.e: After Glaukias the Taulantian kingdom faded from view. By the later 3rd century BCE their lands lay within the Illyrian Kingdom of Agron and Teuta, and after 229 BCE much of the coast came under Roman protection.

tungri.t: People of eastern Belgium who settled the former land of the Eburones and whose town Atuatuca Tungrorum became Tongeren.
tungri.o: After Caesar destroyed the Eburones in 53 BCE, new groups settled the area between the Meuse and the Rhine. Tacitus says the Tungri were the first Germani to cross the Rhine, and that the name Germani spread from them to all their kin.
tungri.r: Their chief town Atuatuca Tungrorum was founded under Augustus and grew into a walled city on the road from Bavay to Cologne. Tungrian cohorts served across the empire, most famously on Hadrian's Wall and at Vindolanda.
tungri.e: The region suffered Frankish raids from the 3rd century, and Tongeren was rebuilt with a smaller wall. In the 4th century it became the seat of Bishop Servatius, whose see later moved to Maastricht and then Liège. Tongeren claims to be the oldest town in Belgium.

tiberina-republic.t: A short-lived republic proclaimed in Perugia in 1798, quickly absorbed into the French-backed Roman Republic.
tiberina-republic.o: In February 1798, as French troops overthrew papal rule in Rome, patriots in Perugia and the upper Tiber valley proclaimed a republic named after the river, taking over the government of Perugia and nearby Umbrian towns.
tiberina-republic.r: Known mainly from local records, the Tiberina Republic was a provisional government of local patriots under French protection. It replaced papal officials, planted liberty trees and adopted republican symbols.
tiberina-republic.e: Within weeks, in 1798, it was merged into the Roman Republic (1798–1799), and Perugia became a department capital of that state.

thasos.t: North Aegean island colony of Paros that grew rich from gold mines and wine, and whose revolt in 465 BCE was crushed by Athens.
thasos.o: Colonists from Paros, among them the poet Archilochus, settled Thasos c. 680 BCE, displacing Thracian inhabitants. The Thasians soon gained a foothold on the facing Thracian mainland, with its gold and silver mines near Mount Pangaion.
thasos.r: Thasos drew wealth from gold mines on the island and the mainland, marble quarries and wine, exported in stamped amphorae across the Aegean and Black Sea. It had an oligarchic government and built strong walls with sculpted gates. The painter Polygnotus was Thasian. The island submitted to Persia in 491 BCE and then joined the Delian League.
thasos.e: When Athens challenged its mainland mines, Thasos revolted in 465 BCE and surrendered to Cimon after a two-year siege, losing its fleet and walls. It later passed under Macedonian rule, was freed by Rome in 196 BCE and kept free status under Roman control.

taifa-of-lorca.t: A minor taifa in the frontier town of Lorca, between Murcia and Almería, independent for some four decades in the 11th century.
taifa-of-lorca.o: Around 1051 local rulers made Lorca and its castle independent, breaking away from the authority exercised over the region by Almería and the Taifa of Murcia during the fragmentation of the 11th century.
taifa-of-lorca.r: Little is recorded beyond its outline. The state centred on Lorca's great hilltop fortress and the irrigated Guadalentín valley. It lay close to the Castilian stronghold of Aledo, held from 1086, which raided the surrounding lands.
taifa-of-lorca.e: Lorca fell to the Almoravids around 1091 together with Murcia and Almería. It later passed to Castile in 1244 and became a frontier town facing the Emirate of Granada.

tarbelli.t: Aquitanian people of the Adour basin and the Landes coast, known for river gold and the hot springs of Dax.
tarbelli.o: The Tarbelli were one of the Aquitani, the peoples between the Garonne and the Pyrenees who spoke a language related to Basque. They held the lower Adour valley and the Atlantic shore around modern Dax and Bayonne. Known chiefly from Caesar, Strabo and Pliny.
tarbelli.r: Strabo describes rich gold deposits in their land, with nuggets found in shallow pits and river sands. Their hot springs at Aquae Tarbellicae (Dax) became famous under Rome. No central capital is recorded before the Roman period.
tarbelli.e: The Tarbelli submitted to Caesar's legate Publius Crassus in 56 BCE after his campaign in Aquitania. Under Augustus they formed a civitas with Aquae Tarbellicae as its chief town, which later became the seat of the bishops of Dax.

taifa-of-huelva.t: A small Arab-ruled taifa on the Odiel estuary, home of the Bakri family whose son became the great geographer Abu Ubayd al-Bakri.
taifa-of-huelva.o: Around 1012, during the collapse of caliphal power, the Arab family of the Banu Bakr made themselves independent in Huelva and the island town of Saltés at the mouth of the Odiel and Tinto rivers. Their founder was Abu Zayd Muhammad ibn Ayyub al-Bakri.
taifa-of-huelva.r: The taifa was a coastal principality living from fishing, salt and the iron industry of Saltés, which exported metalwork along the Atlantic coast. Its rulers balanced between the neighbouring Taifa of Niebla and the Taifa of Seville. The family was cultured: Abu Ubayd al-Bakri, son of the last ruler, later wrote the Book of Roads and Kingdoms.
taifa-of-huelva.e: In 1051 the Abbadid ruler al-Mutadid of Seville forced the last ruler, Abd al-Aziz al-Bakri, to give up Huelva and Saltés. The family moved to Córdoba, where Abu Ubayd built his scholarly career.

tembe-kingdom.t: A Tsonga kingdom on Delagoa Bay that traded ivory with Europeans for three centuries before its lands were split between Portugal and Britain.
tembe-kingdom.o: The Tembe dynasty ruled the southern shore of Delagoa Bay from at least the mid-16th century, when Portuguese shipwreck survivors recorded its chiefs. In the 18th century a branch, the Maputo or Mabudu, became dominant south of the bay and expanded towards the Lubombo mountains.
tembe-kingdom.r: Tembe kings drew wealth from controlling the ivory trade of Delagoa Bay, dealing with Portuguese, English, Dutch and Austrian merchants, and from cattle and farming. Under Makasana in the late 18th and early 19th centuries the kingdom was a strong regional power, but it later paid tribute to the Zulu Kingdom and contended with Swazi and Gaza Nguni pressure.
tembe-kingdom.e: The 1875 MacMahon arbitration awarded Delagoa Bay to Portugal. In the 1890s the kingdom was divided along the new border, with the south (Maputaland) joining British Zululand and the north conquered by Portugal in 1895.

third-taifa-of-murcia.t: The realm of Ibn Hud, who briefly united al-Andalus against the Almohads, and of his heirs, who ended as Castilian vassals in Murcia.
third-taifa-of-murcia.o: In 1228 Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Hud, claiming descent from the Hudids of Zaragoza, rose against the Almohads in the Ricote valley. He recognised the Abbasid caliph, took the title al-Mutawakkil, and within months most of al-Andalus, including Seville, Córdoba and Granada, accepted his rule.
third-taifa-of-murcia.r: Ibn Hud's popularity rested on rejecting Almohad doctrine and promising relief from taxes, but his armies lost to León at Alange in 1230 and Córdoba fell to Castile in 1236. He was murdered in Almería in 1238, and his realm shrank to Murcia. By the Treaty of Alcaraz of 1243 Murcia became a protectorate of the Crown of Castile.
third-taifa-of-murcia.e: The Mudéjar revolt of 1264 drew a Castilian and Aragonese response: James I of Aragon took Murcia in 1266 for Castile, and the territory became the Kingdom of Murcia.

twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A rival Libyan line of kings in Upper Egypt, born from the civil wars that broke up the Twenty-second Dynasty.
twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Around 837 BCE, amid conflict in the Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt, Pedubast I proclaimed himself king and was recognised at Thebes. Manetho linked the dynasty with Tanis, while earlier scholars placed it at Leontopolis; many Egyptologists now see it as a mainly Theban and Upper Egyptian line, but its extent is debated.
twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The dynasty shared power with the Bubastite kings and local Libyan chiefs, each controlling cities and temples. Osorkon III and his son Takelot III ruled as co-regents and placed family members as high priests and as God's Wife of Amun at Thebes. Royal monuments are few, but Theban inscriptions record Nile flood levels and priestly appointments by year of each king.
twenty-third-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 735 BCE Thebes passed under the Kushite Empire. Shepenupet I, daughter of Osorkon III and God's Wife of Amun, adopted Amenirdis I, sister of the Kushite king Piye. Rudamun's line ended as minor rulers, and Iuput II of Leontopolis submitted to Piye.

taifa-of-murviedro.t: A fleeting principality at Murviedro, the old Saguntum, held by a Valencian notable during the turmoil around El Cid's campaigns.
taifa-of-murviedro.o: After the collapse of the Taifa of Valencia's independence and the installation of al-Qadir as a Castilian client in 1086, the Valencian notable Abu Isa ibn Labbun made himself master of the fortress town of Murviedro, the ancient Saguntum, north of Valencia.
taifa-of-murviedro.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, the lordship was little more than the castle and its district. Ibn Labbun manoeuvred between al-Qadir, the Taifa of Albarracín and El Cid, paying tribute to survive.
taifa-of-murviedro.e: By about 1092 Ibn Labbun had handed the town to the ruler of Albarracín. El Cid captured Murviedro in 1098, adding it to the Lordship of Valencia, before it passed to the Almoravids.

tarcondimotid-cilicia.t: The Tarcondimotid kingdom, a Roman client state in the Amanus mountains of eastern Cilicia, loyal to Mark Antony.
tarcondimotid-cilicia.o: Tarcondimotus, a local ruler in the Amanus mountains of eastern Cilicia, supported Pompey when Rome reorganised the region in 64 BCE and was recognised as dynast. He later took the title king, ruling from Hierapolis-Castabala.
tarcondimotid-cilicia.r: The kingdom controlled the passes between Cilicia and Syria and the plain around Castabala. Tarcondimotus I called himself Philantonios, friend of Antony, and supplied ships and troops to his patrons. Coins with his portrait and Greek titles survive.
tarcondimotid-cilicia.e: Tarcondimotus I died fighting for Antony in 31 BCE. Augustus later restored his son Tarcondimotus II Philopator, whose death in 17 CE led Rome to absorb the kingdom into its provinces.

turones.t: Gallic people of the middle Loire whose Roman town Caesarodunum became Tours.
turones.o: The Turones lived along the Loire around modern Tours, between the Carnutes, the Andecavi and the Bituriges Cubi. Caesar mentions them among the peoples where he quartered legions and among those who joined the revolt of 52 BCE.
turones.r: Little is known of their society beyond their oppida and coinage.
turones.e: Under Rome their chief town was Caesarodunum, later called Civitas Turonorum, from which comes Tours. In the 4th century it became the see of Saint Martin of Tours, and his shrine made it one of the great pilgrimage centres of Gaul.

thespiae.t: Boeotian city below Mount Helicon, whose seven hundred citizens stood with the Spartans at Thermopylae and which honoured Eros and the Muses.
thespiae.o: Thespiae lay in the plain of southern Boeotia below Mount Helicon. It developed in the early Iron Age and became one of the larger Boeotian cities, often resisting the domination of Thebes. Its territory included the Valley of the Muses and the port of Creusis.
thespiae.r: Thespiae's chief cult honoured Eros, whose statue by Praxiteles later drew visitors, and it held the Mouseia festival for the Muses. In 480 BCE seven hundred Thespians under Demophilus fought and died at Thermopylae, and the Persians burned the city. Thespiae joined the Boeotian League but was frequently at odds with Thebes.
thespiae.e: Thebes pulled down its walls in 423 BCE and destroyed it c. 373 BCE. Rebuilt under Macedonian protection, it continued as a cultural centre and passed under Rome in 146 BCE.
thespiae.re: Greek religion; cults of Eros and the Muses

turkestan-assr.t: The first Soviet republic in Central Asia, created from Russian Turkestan and divided into the national republics in 1924.
turkestan-assr.o: After the Tashkent Soviet took power in late 1917 and crushed the Kokand Autonomy, the Turkestan Soviet Republic was proclaimed in April 1918 within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic, covering the former Turkestan Governorate-General. Cut off by civil war fronts until 1919, it was at first dominated by Russian settlers.
turkestan-assr.r: Moscow's Turkestan Commission, sent in 1919, curbed settler chauvinism and brought Muslim communists into government, including Turar Ryskulov. The republic fought the Basmachi revolts in Ferghana and famine, and introduced land reform. It governed from Tashkent, with the Bukharan and Khorezm republics as neighbours.
turkestan-assr.e: In the national delimitation of 1924 the republic was dissolved and its territory split among the Uzbek SSR, the Turkmen SSR, the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast, the Tajik ASSR and the Kazakh ASSR. This drew the outlines of today's Central Asian states.

transcaspian-government.t: An anti-Bolshevik government of railway workers and Socialist Revolutionaries in Ashgabat, remembered for the execution of the 26 Baku Commissars.
transcaspian-government.o: In July 1918 railway workers and Socialist Revolutionaries in Ashgabat overthrew the local Soviet authorities of the Turkestan ASSR, forming the Transcaspian Provisional Government under Fyodor Funtikov. Facing Red forces from Tashkent, it appealed for help to the British in Persia.
transcaspian-government.r: The government controlled the Trans-Caspian railway from Krasnovodsk towards Merv, relying on Turkmen and Russian volunteers and a small British force under General Wilfrid Malleson. In September 1918 its men shot the 26 Baku Commissars in the desert east of Krasnovodsk, an event that became a major Soviet symbol of British intervention.
transcaspian-government.e: After the British withdrew in 1919, the Red Army advanced along the railway, taking Ashgabat in July 1919 and Krasnovodsk in February 1920. Transcaspia returned to the Turkestan ASSR and later became the Turkmen SSR.

twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The kings of Tanis who ruled northern Egypt after the New Kingdom, sharing the country with the priests of Amun at Thebes.
twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.o: On the death of Ramesses XI around 1077 BCE, Smendes, who had governed the north from the Delta, became king and founded the Twenty-first Dynasty. The capital moved to Tanis in the north-eastern Delta, built largely from monuments carried from the abandoned Ramesside capital Pi-Ramesses.
twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Tanite kings ruled Lower and Middle Egypt, while the Theocracy of Amun at Thebes governed the south with family ties to them. Tanis was laid out as a northern Thebes with a great temple of Amun. The intact royal tombs found there by Pierre Montet in 1939 to 1940 include the silver coffin and gold mask of Psusennes I. Siamun campaigned in Philistia, and Osorkon the Elder was a Libyan.
twenty-first-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 943 BCE Sheshonq I, a Libyan chief of the Meshwesh and relative by marriage of the last king, Psusennes II, succeeded peacefully and founded the Twenty-second Dynasty of Egypt.

tervingi.t: Gothic people north of the lower Danube whose flight from the Huns in 376 led to the Roman disaster at Adrianople.
tervingi.o: The Tervingi are first named in 291 as a branch of the Goths living between the Danube and the Dniester, in former Roman Dacia and Moldavia. They emerged from the Gothic peoples who had raided the empire through the 3rd century and settled after Rome abandoned Dacia around 271.
tervingi.r: They were ruled by tribal leaders under an overall judge (iudex), the best known being Athanaric. A treaty with Constantine in 332 made them Roman allies and opened trade. Christianity spread among them through Ulfilas, who translated the Bible into Gothic, and Athanaric persecuted Christians in 369–372. Valens fought them in 367–369.
tervingi.e: In 376 the Huns attacked, and a large group under Fritigern was admitted across the Danube. Roman mistreatment led to war, and in 378 they destroyed Valens's army at Adrianople. They later formed the core of the Visigoths.

tercia-pars-regni.t: The ducatus, a third of the Hungarian kingdom ruled by princes of the Árpád dynasty, which fuelled civil wars until abolished by Coloman.
tercia-pars-regni.o: In 1048 King Andrew I granted a third of the Kingdom of Hungary (1000-1301) to his brother Béla, as a ducatus, or duchy. It covered two blocks: one around Nyitra (Nitra) in the north-west and one around Bihar in the east.
tercia-pars-regni.r: The duke held royal revenues, counties and castles in his third, struck his own coins and kept his own retinue. The arrangement made the duke heir presumptive, but it repeatedly led to war: Béla took the throne from Andrew in 1060, and Géza and Ladislaus fought King Solomon in the 1070s.
tercia-pars-regni.e: King Coloman ended the arrangement, taking the duchy from his brother Álmos in 1107. The territory returned to the crown, and Álmos was later blinded with his son Béla.

teutonic-order-mergentheim.t: The Teutonic Order's headquarters at Mergentheim, from which, after losing Prussia in 1525, it governed its scattered lands for nearly three centuries.
teutonic-order-mergentheim.o: When Grand Master Albert secularised Prussia in 1525, the order's German master, Walter von Cronberg, who resided at Mergentheim in Franconia, was made administrator of the grand mastership in 1527, and his successors combined both offices as Hoch- und Deutschmeister. Mergentheim became the order's seat and the capital of its territories within the empire.
teutonic-order-mergentheim.r: The grand master ranked as a prince of the empire and ruled the district around Mergentheim as well as commanderies grouped into bailiwicks across Germany, Austria and beyond. The knights, nobles bound by vows, served as officers in imperial armies against the Ottomans. From the late 16th century the office usually went to Habsburg archdukes or Wittelsbach princes, and Mergentheim castle was rebuilt in Baroque style.
teutonic-order-mergentheim.e: Napoleon dissolved the order in the states of the Confederation of the Rhine in 1809, and Württemberg annexed Mergentheim, suppressing a local uprising. The order survived in Austria and since 1929 has continued as a clerical order with its seat in Vienna.

thessalian-league.t: Federation of the cities of Thessaly, famous for its cavalry, which elected a war leader called the tagos and was later dominated by Macedon.
thessalian-league.o: The plains of Thessaly were ruled by landowning families such as the Aleuadae of Larissa. By the 6th century BCE the cities formed a league with the neighbouring perioikoi peoples. Aleuas the Red was credited with organising Thessaly into four districts, each supplying cavalry and hoplites.
thessalian-league.r: In wartime the league elected a tagos as commander. Thessalian cavalry was the best in Greece, and the economy rested on grain and horses worked by serfs called penestai. The Thessalians sided with Persia in 480 BCE. Jason of Pherae, elected tagos c. 370 BCE, briefly made Thessaly a great power before his murder.
thessalian-league.e: Philip II was made archon of the league in the 340s BCE, and Macedonian kings held the post thereafter. Rome restored a Thessalian League centred on Larissa in 196 BCE, and it continued under Roman control from 146 BCE.

tricasses.t: Small Gallic people of the upper Seine whose Roman town Augustobona became Troyes.
tricasses.o: The Tricasses are not mentioned by Caesar and were probably dependents of the Senones in his time. Pliny and Ptolemy record them as a separate people on the Seine in Champagne.
tricasses.r: Nothing is known of their pre-Roman institutions.
tricasses.e: Under Rome they formed a civitas with Augustobona as its chief town, later called Trecae after the people, the origin of Troyes. Bishop Lupus of Troyes is said to have negotiated with Attila in 451, and the city became capital of the County of Champagne.

taifa-of-albarracin.t: A mountain taifa in the Sierra de Albarracín ruled for nearly a century by the Berber Banu Razin, one of the longest-lived small states of al-Andalus.
taifa-of-albarracin.o: The Banu Razin, a Berber family of the Hawwara who had held the district of al-Sahla since the 8th century, declared independence around 1012 under Hudhayl ibn Khalaf ibn Razin as the Caliphate of Córdoba broke apart.
taifa-of-albarracin.r: Albarracín was a rugged frontier lordship of castles, pasture and timber between the taifas of Toledo, Zaragoza and Valencia. Its survival owed much to the long reign of Abd al-Malik ibn Hudhayl (c. 1045-1103), who paid tribute to Castile and to El Cid when necessary. The town's walls and its compact old quarter date in part from this period.
taifa-of-albarracin.e: The Almoravids annexed Albarracín in 1104, soon after the death of Abd al-Malik. In 1170 the Navarrese noble Pedro Ruiz de Azagra received the town, founding the semi-independent Lordship of Albarracín.

taifa-of-mertola.t: A tiny taifa on the Guadiana at Mértola, an old river port in southern Portugal, independent for little more than a decade.
taifa-of-mertola.o: Around 1033 a local leader, known as Ibn Tayfur, made Mértola and its district independent, in the period when the small principalities of the south-west were breaking away from both the Hammudids and the Taifa of Badajoz.
taifa-of-mertola.r: Known only from brief references in Arabic chronicles, the state consisted of the hilltop town and its castle above the Guadiana, the highest navigable point for river traffic from the Atlantic, with copper and grain trade.
taifa-of-mertola.e: Around 1044 al-Mutadid of the Taifa of Seville annexed Mértola. A century later it became the base of the Sufi rebel Ibn Qasi, as the Second Taifa of Mértola.

third-taifa-of-valencia.t: The last Muslim kingdom of Valencia under Zayyan ibn Mardanish, which fell to James I of Aragon in 1238.
third-taifa-of-valencia.o: In 1229 Zayyan ibn Mardanish, a descendant of the Wolf King of the Second Taifa of Murcia, overthrew the Almohad governor of Valencia, Abu Zayd. Abu Zayd fled to James I of Aragon, later converting to Christianity and helping his campaigns.
third-taifa-of-valencia.r: Zayyan ruled the city and the irrigated huerta with its rice, sugar and silk, recognising the Abbasids. His position was weak: he faced Ibn Hud's rival power in Murcia and the steady advance of Aragonese forces, which won at the Puig in 1237.
third-taifa-of-valencia.e: After a siege, Zayyan surrendered Valencia to James I on 28 September 1238, and the Muslim population was allowed to leave. The city became the capital of the Kingdom of Valencia. Zayyan withdrew to Dénia and later Murcia.

triballi.t: Powerful Thracian people of the Morava and Iskar valleys who killed an Odrysian king, wounded Philip II and defied Alexander the Great.
triballi.o: The Triballi held the plains south of the Danube between the Morava and Iskar rivers, in modern eastern Serbia and north-western Bulgaria, by the 5th century BCE. Greek historians treat them as one of the largest Thracian peoples, independent of the Odrysian Kingdom.
triballi.r: Ruled by kings and war leaders, they were feared raiders. In 424 BCE the Odrysian king Sitalces died fighting them, and in 376 BCE they attacked Abdera on the Aegean. In 339 BCE they ambushed Philip II returning from Scythia, wounding him and seizing his booty. In 335 BCE Alexander defeated them, and their king Syrmus took refuge on the Danube island of Peuce before submitting.
triballi.e: Defeats by the Autariatae and later the Celtic Scordisci weakened them. Rome conquered the region when Marcus Licinius Crassus campaigned in 29 BCE, and their land became part of Moesia.

taifa-of-menorca.t: An autonomous Muslim island state that survived for half a century as a tributary of Aragon after the Christian conquest of Majorca.
taifa-of-menorca.o: After James I of Aragon took Majorca in 1229, the Muslim leaders of Menorca agreed in 1231, by the Treaty of Capdepera, to recognise him as overlord and pay tribute, while keeping their own government, law and religion. The island was known in Arabic as Manurqa.
taifa-of-menorca.r: The island was ruled by a ra'is from Madina Manurqa, the later Ciutadella. Abu Uthman Said ibn Hakam (ruled 1234-1282), a scholar and poet, gathered a library and kept the island prosperous through farming, livestock and trade with North Africa while paying tribute to Aragon.
taifa-of-menorca.e: In January 1287 Alfonso III of Aragon invaded, accusing the island of aiding the Hafsid Sultanate. Most inhabitants were enslaved or expelled, and Menorca was resettled by Catalans as part of the Kingdom of Majorca.

taifa-of-lerida.t: A Hudid taifa at Lleida on the Segre, a frontier state facing the Catalan counties that at times rivalled its parent state, Zaragoza.
taifa-of-lerida.o: Lleida belonged to the Upper March governed from Zaragoza. Around 1039 it came under Sulayman ibn Hud, founder of the Hudid dynasty, and on his death in 1046 his son Yusuf al-Muzaffar ruled it as an independent kingdom, fighting his brother al-Muqtadir of the Taifa of Zaragoza.
taifa-of-lerida.r: The taifa controlled the fertile Segre valley and bordered the County of Barcelona and the County of Urgell, to whom it paid tribute. Under al-Mundhir (1081-1090) it was joined with Tortosa and Dénia, and he employed El Cid against Barcelona and his own nephew in Zaragoza.
taifa-of-lerida.e: Lleida passed under Almoravid control around 1110. In 1149 Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona and Ermengol VI of Urgell captured the city, adding it to what became the Principality of Catalonia.

turkestan-governorate-general.t: The Russian colonial government of Central Asia, ruled from Tashkent, which turned the region's oases into a cotton economy.
turkestan-governorate-general.o: After Russian forces took Tashkent in 1865, the Turkestan Governorate-General was created in 1867 under General Konstantin von Kaufmann. It expanded through the conquest of Samarkand in 1868, the Khanate of Kokand in 1876 and the Turkmen lands after the storming of Geok Tepe in 1881.
turkestan-governorate-general.r: The governor-general held wide military and civil powers, with the Emirate of Bukhara and the Khanate of Khiva left as protectorates. Russia built the Trans-Caspian and Orenburg-Tashkent railways and promoted American cotton, which became the region's main crop. Muslim courts and customs were mostly left in place, but Russian settlers took land on the steppe. The Jadid movement campaigned for educational reform.
turkestan-governorate-general.e: A revolt in 1916 against wartime labour conscription was brutally suppressed. After the Russian Revolution of 1917 the Tashkent Soviet seized power, and the region became the Turkestan ASSR in 1918.

tunip.t: Tunip, a Syrian city of the Orontes valley caught between Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites in the Late Bronze Age.
tunip.o: Tunip lay in the Orontes region of western Syria; its site is uncertain. It appears in the 15th century BCE among the cities that resisted Thutmose III of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom, as an ally of Kadesh and the Mitanni Empire.
tunip.r: Little is known of its government, though a council of citizens appears to have shared power. In the Amarna letters, the people of Tunip wrote to the pharaoh begging him to restore the son of their former ruler and protect them from Aziru of the Kingdom of Amurru.
tunip.e: Tunip passed under Hittite control in the 14th century BCE. Ramesses II attacked it during his Syrian wars, and it fades from the record in the 13th century BCE.

taifa-of-jaen.t: A taifa in the upper Guadalquivir held by the warlord Ibn Hamushk, father-in-law and ally of the Wolf King, Ibn Mardanish.
taifa-of-jaen.o: In 1145, during the collapse of Almoravid rule, Jaén and its region came under local rebels. The most durable was Ibrahim ibn Hamushk, a commander who held Jaén and the castles of the Sierra de Segura and allied himself with Muhammad ibn Mardanish.
taifa-of-jaen.r: Jaén was a land of olive groves and frontier fortresses facing Castile and the Almohads. Ibn Hamushk was a military strongman who at times took Granada and fought both Christian and Almohad forces, while relying on the wealth and mercenaries of the Second Taifa of Murcia.
taifa-of-jaen.e: Around 1159 Jaén passed to the Almohads. Ibn Hamushk later broke with Ibn Mardanish and joined the Almohads himself. Ferdinand III of the Crown of Castile took Jaén in 1246.

travunia.t: Small Slavic principality around Trebinje in eastern Herzegovina, ruled by local lords under Serbian, Byzantine and Dukljan overlords.
travunia.o: Travunia formed in the 7th to 9th centuries among Serbs settled in the hinterland of Dubrovnik. Constantine VII records that its ruler Krajina, son of Beloje, married the daughter of the Serbian prince Vlastimir in the 9th century, tying it to the Principality of Serbia (early medieval).
travunia.r: Ruled by hereditary župans from Trebinje, it had towns such as Risan and controlled routes from the coast into the interior. It was usually dependent on a larger neighbour: Serbia, Byzantium, and from the 11th century Duklja, whose rulers often installed relatives there.
travunia.e: Grand Župan Stefan Nemanja of the Grand Principality of Serbia annexed Travunia, with Duklja, around 1186. It remained part of the Serbian lands, later passing to Bosnia, and its centre Trebinje is now in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

taifa-of-malaga.t: The Hammudid taifa of Málaga, ruled by a Berberised Arab dynasty that claimed the caliphate of al-Andalus after the Umayyads fell.
taifa-of-malaga.o: The Hammudids, descendants of the Idrisids of Morocco, had briefly held the caliphate in Córdoba from 1016. Driven from the capital, they made Málaga their base around 1026, when Yahya ibn Ali al-Mutali established his court there while still claiming the title of caliph.
taifa-of-malaga.r: The Hammudids led the Berber party in the fitna and were recognised as caliphs by several Berber taifas, including Ronda and Carmona. Their state, spanning Málaga and at times Algeciras and Ceuta, was weakened by succession quarrels, and real power often lay with Berber commanders and the Zirids of Granada.
taifa-of-malaga.e: In 1057 Badis of the Taifa of Granada annexed Málaga, ending the Hammudid line in al-Andalus. The city was later briefly independent again as the Second Taifa of Málaga under a Zirid prince.

triarchy-of-negroponte.t: Crusader lordship on Euboea, split among three Lombard lords under the growing shadow of Venice, which eventually took over the whole island.
triarchy-of-negroponte.o: After the Fourth Crusade, Boniface of Montferrat granted Euboea in 1205 to Jacques d'Avesnes and then to Lombard nobles from Verona, notably Ravano dalle Carceri. In 1209 Ravano recognised Venetian overlordship. After his death in 1216 the island was divided into three parts, the terzieri, each held by a lord called a triarch.
triarchy-of-negroponte.r: The triarchs, of families such as the dalle Carceri and Ghisi, were vassals of the Principality of Achaea but relied on Venice, which held quarters and a bailo in the town of Negroponte (Chalcis) and controlled its trade. Greek peasants worked the land under Latin lords. The renegade knight Licario, serving Byzantium, recaptured much of the island in the 1270s.
triarchy-of-negroponte.e: Threatened by the Catalans of the Duchy of Athens and the Turks, the triarchs ceded more and more to Venice. By 1390 Venice ruled the whole island directly as Venetian Negroponte.

third-taifa-of-niebla.t: The last independent Muslim state of western al-Andalus, ruled by Ibn Mahfuz from Niebla until Alfonso X took it in 1262.
third-taifa-of-niebla.o: Around 1234, as Ibn Hud's power faded, Shuayb ibn Muhammad ibn Mahfuz established himself in Niebla and the surrounding district as an independent ruler. After Ferdinand III took Seville in 1248, he accepted Castilian overlordship and paid tribute.
third-taifa-of-niebla.r: The small realm covered Niebla, Huelva and the lower Guadiana region, protected by Niebla's massive walls. As a vassal of the Crown of Castile, Ibn Mahfuz kept internal autonomy, but his isolation between Castilian Seville and the Kingdom of Portugal left him little room to manoeuvre.
third-taifa-of-niebla.e: In 1262 Alfonso X besieged Niebla for several months, and Ibn Mahfuz surrendered in exchange for lands and income in Seville. The territory became part of Castile.

taifa-of-denia.t: A maritime taifa that ruled the Balearic Islands and raided Sardinia, founded by the freedman Mujahid al-Amiri on the Valencian coast.
taifa-of-denia.o: Mujahid al-Amiri, a freedman of the Amirid household, seized Dénia around 1010 during the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba. He soon added the Balearic Islands and briefly set up a puppet caliph, al-Muaiti, to give his rule legitimacy.
taifa-of-denia.r: Dénia was a naval power. In 1015-1016 Mujahid's fleet invaded Sardinia before being driven out by Pisa and Genoa. The port traded across the western Mediterranean, and the court supported Quranic scholarship: Abu Amr al-Dani, the leading authority on Quran recitation, worked there. Under Ali Iqbal al-Dawla the state kept close ties with Egypt.
taifa-of-denia.e: In 1076 al-Muqtadir of the Taifa of Zaragoza annexed Dénia, while the Balearics broke away under their governor as the Taifa of Majorca. Dénia later fell to the Almoravids and in 1244 to the Crown of Aragon.

tricastini.t: Gallic people of the Rhône valley near Montélimar through whose land Hannibal marched towards the Alps in 218 BCE.
tricastini.o: The Tricastini lived east of the Rhône in the modern Drôme, around Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux. Livy names them on Hannibal's route after he crossed the Rhône in 218 BCE.
tricastini.r: Almost nothing is known of their society. Their position between the Cavares and the Vocontii placed them on the routes from the Rhône into the Alps.
tricastini.e: After the Roman conquest of 121 BCE they became part of Gallia Narbonensis. Their town was refounded as Augusta Tricastinorum, the origin of Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux, and the name lives on in the Tricastin district.
